item.title: Wall Street’s Three Stooges: The AI Economy and the Twenty-Dollar Bill
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Artificial intelligence may be the technological revolution of our lifetime. The financial machinery built around it, however, increasingly resembles a vaudeville routine. item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence may be the technological revolution of our lifetime. The financial machinery built around it, however, increasingly resembles a vaudeville routine.

There is an old Three Stooges routine that, in retrospect, might be one of the finest explanations of modern American capitalism ever committed to film.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Moe finds a twenty-dollar bill. Larry taps him on the shoulder and reminds him that he owes him twenty dollars. Moe acknowledges the debt and hands him the bill.

Curly then reminds Larry that he owes him twenty dollars. Larry hands him the bill.

Finally, Moe reminds Curly that he owes him twenty dollars. Curly hands the bill back to Moe.

Three transactions. Sixty dollars in payments. One twenty-dollar bill.

And Moe ends up exactly where he started.

The remarkable thing about this little routine is that the Three Stooges actually accomplished something economically useful: they extinguished sixty dollars in outstanding debt using twenty dollars in available liquidity.

Now imagine the same routine performed by Silicon Valley’s biggest corporations, with Wall Street providing the laugh track.

The Magnificent Seven and the Twenty-Dollar Bill

In Brazil, we have a traditional children’s game called Escravos de Jó. The participants sit in a circle, passing objects from one person to another in rhythm with a song.

Watching the financial relationships developing around the artificial intelligence industry, I cannot help but be reminded of that game.

Except that instead of children passing stones around a table, we have multibillion-dollar corporations passing enormous bags of money around an increasingly interconnected financial ecosystem.

A semiconductor manufacturer invests billions in an artificial intelligence company.

The artificial intelligence company commits billions to purchasing computing capacity from a cloud provider.

The cloud provider purchases billions in processors from the semiconductor manufacturer.

The semiconductor manufacturer announces unprecedented demand for its products.

The cloud provider announces unprecedented demand for its infrastructure.

The artificial intelligence company announces unprecedented investment in its future.

Wall Street celebrates all three announcements.

Stock prices soar. Analysts revise their projections. Executives congratulate themselves. Financial journalists proclaim the dawn of a new economic paradigm.

And somewhere in the middle of this corporate choreography, the same capital has effectively financed several different transactions.

This is a simplified illustration of circular financing, not an allegation that every major technology company is engaged in fraudulent accounting. The transactions can be perfectly legitimate. The processors are real. The computing capacity is real. The infrastructure being built is real.

What remains uncertain is whether the demand ultimately supporting all this investment is sufficient and sustainable independently of the companies financing it.

That is a rather important distinction.

The Problem Begins When Someone Actually Needs to Spend the Money

Let us return to the Three Stooges.

Moe has his twenty-dollar bill back. Everyone has settled their debts. Everything is wonderful.

Then the landlord knocks on the door.

Each of the three owes twenty dollars in rent.

Suddenly, the three men have sixty dollars in external obligations and only twenty dollars between them.

They can pass that bill around the room as many times as they like. They can announce strategic partnerships, establish joint ventures, issue press releases and hire McKinsey to produce a magnificent PowerPoint presentation.

They are still forty dollars short.

That is the problem with confusing the circulation of money with the creation of wealth.

Artificial intelligence requires enormous amounts of physical infrastructure. Data centers require land, concrete, steel, transformers, cooling systems, networking equipment and electricity. Semiconductor manufacturing requires sophisticated machinery, raw materials and highly specialized labor.

Employees need salaries. Creditors expect interest payments. Construction companies expect to be paid.

The electric utility does not accept market capitalization as payment.

Eventually, the money has to leave the circle.

And when it does, it must be replenished by genuine economic activity capable of generating sufficient cash.

That cash can come from customers, from profitable existing businesses, from additional investors or from borrowing. But the latter two cannot indefinitely substitute for a commercially sustainable operation.

At some point, somebody has to make money rather than merely raise it.

Market Capitalization Is Not Money

One of the most peculiar affectations of modern financial journalism is its habit of treating market capitalization as though it were an enormous bank account.

A company supposedly “loses” a hundred billion dollars on Monday and “gains” a hundred and fifty billion dollars on Tuesday.

Where did the money go? Where did it come from?

In many cases, nowhere.

Suppose a corporation has one billion outstanding shares trading at one hundred dollars each. Its market capitalization is one hundred billion dollars.

Investor confidence deteriorates, and the share price falls to seventy dollars.

Thirty billion dollars in market capitalization has evaporated.

Yet the corporation has not necessarily lost thirty billion dollars in cash. Its factories are still there. Its employees are still working. Its intellectual property remains intact.

What changed was the price investors were willing to pay for its shares.

Market capitalization is a valuation, not a measurement of accumulated cash or productive capacity. It incorporates expectations about future profitability, growth, risk and, increasingly, the collective enthusiasm of investors.

Or, to dispense with the sophisticated financial terminology: vibes.

This does not mean stock market valuations are economically irrelevant. They influence borrowing costs, investment decisions, acquisitions, retirement savings and the ability of corporations to raise capital.

That is precisely what makes speculative valuations so dangerous.

An entirely subjective reassessment of future prospects can produce very real consequences in the present.

The Load-Bearing CEO

On November 23, 2026, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had been reinstated as its chief executive officer following his resignation earlier that month.

Nvidia’s shares surged 31.5%. The Nasdaq gained approximately 6.5%. The S&P 500 rose 4.7%.

Nearly a trillion dollars in Nvidia’s market capitalization was restored in a single trading session.

Had Nvidia invented a revolutionary processor overnight?

Had it constructed another semiconductor fabrication facility? Had its productive capacity increased by nearly one-third? Had artificial intelligence suddenly become dramatically more profitable for its customers?

No.

A man had returned to his office.

A YouTube creator discussing the incident coined a particularly appropriate expression: a “load-bearing CEO.”

In software engineering, we have a considerably less amusing term for this phenomenon: a single point of failure.

We spend enormous amounts of time designing critical systems specifically to eliminate single points of failure. We introduce redundancy, failover mechanisms, backups and alternative execution paths because we understand that individual components can and eventually will fail.

A system whose continued operation depends entirely on one irreplaceable component is a badly designed system.

Apparently, Wall Street considers this an investment strategy.

If the departure of one executive can contribute to a widespread financial panic, and his return can restore hundreds of billions of dollars in valuations, we should be examining the fragility of the financial ecosystem rather than merely celebrating the executive’s return.

The existence of a load-bearing CEO is not simply a testament to the individual’s brilliance. It is an indictment of the architecture surrounding him.

We Have Seen This Movie Before

The comparison with the 2008 financial crisis is tempting, although the underlying mechanisms are not identical.

Before 2008, financial institutions accumulated enormous exposure to interconnected financial instruments whose values depended on assumptions about the housing market.

Those instruments were packaged, repackaged, divided and distributed throughout the financial system. Institutions that appeared to have diversified their investments had, in reality, accumulated exposure to many of the same underlying risks.

When those assumptions failed, the apparent diversification offered far less protection than anticipated.

The contemporary artificial intelligence ecosystem presents a different but troubling form of interconnected exposure.

A semiconductor manufacturer finances a company that consumes computing capacity. A cloud provider builds infrastructure in anticipation of that consumption. An AI developer commits to purchasing infrastructure on the assumption that its own customer base will eventually justify the expenditure.

Each participant’s success becomes increasingly dependent upon the success of the others.

If anticipated demand fails to materialize, the consequences need not remain confined to one company.

The AI developer may reduce its computing commitments. The cloud provider may find itself with excess capacity and outstanding construction debt. The semiconductor manufacturer may experience declining orders.

The investors who thought they had diversified their portfolios across several different technology companies may discover that they had effectively made several variations of the same bet.

Correlated financial exposure masquerading as diversification.

Sound familiar?

Artificial Intelligence Is Not the Bubble

I want to make something abundantly clear: this is not an indictment of artificial intelligence.

I am a software developer who uses artificial intelligence professionally, extensively and daily. I have experienced firsthand the extraordinary productivity gains that these technologies can deliver.

I do not need a Wall Street analyst to convince me that artificial intelligence has practical economic value.

But there are four fundamentally different propositions that the financial establishment seems determined to treat as interchangeable:

  • Artificial intelligence is a revolutionary technology.

  • Artificial intelligence can dramatically increase productivity.

  • Artificial intelligence companies can become sustainably profitable.

  • Artificial intelligence companies are worth their current valuations.

The first two can be entirely true while the last two turn out to be spectacularly wrong.

We witnessed precisely this phenomenon during the dot-com bubble.

The Internet did not stop working when the bubble burst. Its usefulness did not suddenly disappear. Its potential to transform commerce, communication and society was not imaginary.

What collapsed was the speculative financial structure that had been erected around it.

Wall Street had correctly identified a revolutionary technology and then proceeded to lose staggering amounts of money by incorrectly valuing the businesses attempting to commercialize it.

Recognizing the technological revolution did not make every investment in it intelligent.

Artificial intelligence is no exception.

When the Music Stops

Unlike many of the companies that populated the dot-com bubble, today’s technology giants possess enormous established businesses capable of generating substantial cash.

Microsoft sells software and cloud services. Alphabet sells advertising. Amazon operates an enormous retail and cloud computing empire. Meta generates advertising revenue. Nvidia sells actual processors.

This provides the industry with considerable financial resilience.

But resilience is not immunity.

The question is whether the returns generated by artificial intelligence will ultimately justify the enormous capital expenditures being undertaken to support it.

If they do, much of this investment may prove extraordinarily profitable.

If they do not, the existence of profitable legacy businesses will not magically transform bad investments into good ones. It will simply determine how much financial punishment those corporations can absorb before they are forced to reconsider their commitments.

And, as usual, the consequences will not necessarily be confined to the executives who authorized those commitments or the investors who enthusiastically encouraged them.

Workers, pension funds, ordinary shareholders, contractors and communities dependent upon promised infrastructure projects may find themselves paying for decisions they never participated in making.

We have seen that movie before, too.

The danger is not that artificial intelligence will turn out to be useless.

The danger is that Wall Street will have once again taken something genuinely useful, inflated its financial expectations beyond what the underlying economics can sustain, and confused the resulting speculative frenzy with the creation of durable wealth.

Moe, Larry and Curly understood that circulating twenty dollars could settle sixty dollars in debts.

Wall Street appears determined to convince itself that circulating twenty dollars can create sixty dollars in wealth.

At least the Three Stooges knew they were performing a comedy.

The real test begins when the landlord knocks on the door.

References

  • Load Bearing CEO — YouTube

  • Nvidia Board Reinstates Jensen Huang as President, CEO and Board Director — November 23, 2026

  • Nvidia’s SEC Form 8-K concerning Huang’s reinstatement

  • US stocks surge after Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia’s CEO — Associated Press

item.content:encoded:
Sean Hannity, not Donald Trump, is emerging as the Republican gatekeeper to watch ahead of 2028. According to AlterNet’s account of a Washington Post profile, the longtime Fox News host plans to interrogate the party’s leading presidential contenders and decide whom to support—an endorsement Hannity portrays as potentially decisive even as Trump’s popularity declines.

That does not make Hannity the party’s formal leader, and the reporting cannot establish four years early who will determine the nomination. It does reveal something more concrete: Republican aspirants are expected to seek approval from a television personality whose power comes from commanding a loyal audience, enforcing ideological boundaries and offering favored politicians sustained protection.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The primary before the primary

Washington Post writer Timothy Bella calls the approaching competition “the Hannity Primary.” Hannity intends to question each major contender, testing not only conservative credentials but electoral viability.

“You could be the perfect conservative, but if you don’t have the ability to win a race, why would I support you?” Hannity said. That formulation places him in the role of strategist and validator, not merely commentator. Candidates must satisfy his definition of conservatism and persuade him that they can convert it into power.

Hannity presents his endorsement as a hard-won seal of approval. Recalling 2016, he described “very long, late-night, deep conversations” with Trump and said he warned the candidate: “If you don’t convince me, I’m not going to vote for you, and I will not support you. Period.”

This account conveniently casts Hannity as a discerning evaluator rather than what he became: one of Trump’s most dependable media advocates. But the distinction matters less than the access itself. Hannity had prolonged private conversations with a presidential candidate, then used one of cable television’s most influential platforms to champion him.

Advocacy packaged as judgment

Hannity’s power is built on the collapse of any meaningful boundary between political coverage and political sponsorship. His Fox program remained among cable news’s five highest-ranked shows even when the network’s broader standing suffered, according to AlterNet. That audience gives him something party officials cannot easily replicate: repeated access to Republican voters inside a trusted partisan environment.

Stephen A. Smith put the relationship bluntly: “I don’t think Trump would have become president without Sean.” Smith described Hannity as relentlessly protective of the people he supports, willing to erect “a ton of brick walls” between them and their critics.

Dan Bongino, identified in the report as a radio host and former FBI deputy director, offered a more qualified assessment. Trump “would have been fine on his own,” he said, but Hannity’s early support helped launch what became the MAGA movement—a political project Bongino said many people hope will survive Trump.

Neither comment proves that Hannity single-handedly produced Trump’s victory. They do, however, describe a media figure acting as political infrastructure: selecting allies, amplifying them and shielding them once selected. Hannity’s influence does not depend on holding office because elected Republicans depend on reaching the audience he has cultivated.

Loyalty without accountability

The substance of Hannity’s record matters as much as the size of his platform. AlterNet notes that he remained beside Trump through repeated controversies, including Trump’s questioning of election legitimacy when results went against him.

Hannity’s response to criticism is not reconsideration but self-exoneration. “We’ve been vindicated more times than I can count,” he told the Post. He treats that asserted record as the source of his credibility and, therefore, as the reason candidates seek his backing.

Fox host Laura Ingraham praised Hannity’s ability to understand people’s needs and navigate politics and culture, calling him both an analyst and an entertainer. That combination is precisely what makes his role politically potent. Entertainment supplies intimacy and loyalty; analysis supplies the appearance of independent judgment. The endorsement then arrives carrying both.

Hannity’s claim that a 2028 candidate cannot prevail without him remains a boast, not an established fact. His retrospective certainty—“I felt Donald Trump could win, and I was not wrong”—also turns one correct political judgment into a sweeping claim of authority.

Still, Republican contenders who submit to the “Hannity Primary” will help make the boast real. The power here is not mystical and does not belong to Hannity alone. It is produced by candidates who treat a cable host as a necessary broker, a network that supplies the platform and a party whose voters have been trained to receive political advocacy as news analysis. Trump may eventually leave the stage. The machinery that promoted and protected him is already auditioning replacements.

item.title: Young Republicans sound off on Trump and GOP at Texas meeting: 'Grow up'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Young Republicans meeting at a Texas brewery after the GOP’s 2026 midterm rout reached an unsparing conclusion: Donald Trump and his party had helped engineer their own defeat through broken promises, economic detachment, personal fealty and behavior several attendees described as childish. item.content:encoded:
Young Republicans meeting at a Texas brewery after the GOP’s 2026 midterm rout reached an unsparing conclusion: Donald Trump and his party had helped engineer their own defeat through broken promises, economic detachment, personal fealty and behavior several attendees described as childish. Their advice—“grow up”—was directed not at wayward voters but at the people who held power and squandered it.

The Monday gathering, organized by the Tarrant County Young Republicans and reported by The Independent, was less a rebellion against Republican politics than an argument over whether the party can function after years organized around Trump. These were activists and voters confronting a loss from inside the coalition, including a three-time Trump supporter, a Republican who sat out the midterms and a state Young Republican leader urging his party to stop blaming everyone else.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A defeat the party cannot blame away

“Everyone has someone to blame, and that finger is never pointed at ourself,” Derrick Wilson, head of the Texas Young Republican Federation, told The Independent. “So we're going to have to get past that and figure out, what did we do wrong?”

That question punctures the reflexive machinery of political scapegoating. Parties in power can blame hostile media, insufficiently loyal officials or an ungrateful electorate. What they cannot honestly do is pretend they lacked agency. According to the Republicans at this meeting, the GOP’s own conduct contributed to its losses.

The local chapter had already registered deeper disaffection before Election Day: its previous leader resigned ahead of the midterms after concluding that she could not vote for her party. Trevor Carr, a 25-year-old attending his first meeting, also sat out the election because he doubted Trump would fulfill his promises. He interpreted the result as a rejection of the party’s old guard and called for a movement built around a durable ideological program rather than allegiance to one man.

Carr credited Trump with disrupting the political establishment a decade earlier but said that period had exhausted itself. “It’s served its purpose, and it’s time to move on to be a serious political movement,” he said.

Affordability exposes the limits of spectacle

Robert Coe, 29, did not arrive as a Trump apostate. He voted for Trump three times and remained loyal to Republicans in the 2026 midterms. Yet he told The Independent that Trump appeared disconnected from the country’s affordability crisis and had offered no credible remedy.

“Me and millions of other Americans are just tired of that, and we’re not seeing any viable solution to it,” Coe said. “It’s almost as if the people in power don’t even want to try and solve it.”

Coe’s frustration identifies the governing failure beneath the party’s style problem. Name-calling and factional combat are not merely embarrassing manners. They consume attention while officials with institutional authority fail to address material pressures facing voters. When politics becomes an endless performance of grievance, spectacle can obscure the absence of results—but it cannot make rent, food or other necessities more affordable.

Coe said he was finished with “the high school-level name-calling” and infighting conducted “on an almost childish level.” He also said the party now lacked “decency.” Other attendees urged Republican leaders to take themselves seriously and show humility.

The loyalty structure is now the liability

The sharpest criticism at the meeting was not simply that Trump had become rude or ineffective. It was that the party had subordinated a coherent political identity to one person, then discovered that personal loyalty could not substitute indefinitely for governing.

Carr wants to help shape the GOP’s future, but his proposed reset would require party officials to surrender the organizing principle that has rewarded them for years: allegiance to Trump. That is a harder demand than asking politicians to improve their tone. It challenges the distribution of influence inside the party, where loyalty has served as a credential and dissent as a liability.

The young Republicans’ diagnosis therefore runs ahead of their prescription. “Grow up” captures their disgust, but maturity is not a policy platform, and humility is not an institutional reform. The officials and operatives who constructed this arrangement still hold the power to decide whether the GOP changes course. The brewery attendees can name the failure. They cannot, by themselves, compel the people who benefited from it to let go.

item.title: Fox unloads on new Trump move everybody hates: 'Are you serious?'

item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration is expanding tariffs on China and dozens of other countries, reviving a policy that Fox Business panelists described Wednesday as an unpopular tax on Americans already struggling with prices. The remarkable part was not that critics objected. It was that the objection came from a network usually hospitable to Trump, where business figures bluntly warned that the president’s tariff campaign is raising costs, disrupting investment and ignoring the political demand for affordability.

The headline-sized answer to who “hates” the move is less universal but more instructive: the Fox panel opposed it, and a Fox News poll cited during the discussion found that 63 percent of voters said tariffs hurt them financially. Trump is proceeding anyway.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The bill does not stop at the border

“A tariff is a tax,” Forbes editor-in-chief Steve Forbes told The Big Money Show. That elementary fact is routinely obscured by political language suggesting tariffs simply make foreign governments pay tribute to Washington. In practice, the federal government collects the charge from importers, and businesses must then absorb the expense, pass it to customers or divide the damage between them.

Marcus Lemonis, who said he owns or participates in several big-box retailers, described precisely that pressure. He already faces difficult pricing decisions and limited room to pass along further increases, he said, making another round of tariffs “very troubling” for the rest of the year and into the next.

That is the policy’s domestic chain of consequence: the White House imposes the tariff, importing companies encounter higher costs, retailers recalculate prices and American households meet the result at the register. Foreign retaliation can then hit US exporters as well. Forbes noted that governments targeted by American tariffs typically answer with tariffs of their own.

The policy also arrives as the Federal Reserve weighs another interest-rate increase while trying to contain inflation. One panelist questioned how Trump could justify adding tariffs immediately before that decision. The White House controls tariff policy; the Fed responds to inflationary conditions. Consumers can be squeezed by both higher prices and more expensive borrowing without controlling either institution.

From trade enforcement to improvisation

Forbes distinguished limited tariffs aimed at specific trade abuses from Trump’s sweeping and unstable approach. He cited Ronald Reagan’s measures against Japanese automakers in the 1980s as an example of targeted action. Trump’s program, he argued, has become something closer to “anarchy.”

His sharper criticism concerned the administration’s apparent determination to preserve the tariff regime through new legal formulations. “If the court strikes down one set of tariffs,” Forbes said, the White House seems prepared to “find an excuse for another.”

Host Cheryl Casone similarly predicted another court fight. She said her reading was that the Supreme Court had already rejected the earlier approach and that the newly announced policy was another version associated with James Grier, whom she identified as one of the architects of the first 2025 tariffs. “See you in court,” Casone said.

Those were the panelists’ legal assessments, not a reported ruling on the new policy. But their description exposes the institutional issue: an administration confronted with legal resistance is not necessarily reconsidering the substance of its program. It is searching for another route to the same result. Courts may decide whether that route is lawful. Businesses must plan before the litigation is resolved.

Volatility is part of the cost

Trump’s tariff policy does not merely raise a price. Its constant reversals make future costs harder to estimate. When Lemonis discussed planning for the coming months, Forbes supplied the bleak punchline: “It will change next week.”

Markets respond to that uncertainty because firms cannot confidently price goods, arrange supply chains or commit capital when the rules may be rewritten by the next presidential announcement. Panelist Lou Basenese called the resulting market turbulence “tariff tantrums” and urged Trump to abandon the policy. His reaction on seeing the latest move was simply: “Are you serious?”

The administration’s defenders may present this unpredictability as negotiating leverage. For companies making purchasing and investment decisions, however, it functions as government-created instability. The president holds the power to initiate the disruption while businesses and consumers are left to insure themselves against his next change of direction.

An affordability message the White House discarded

The Fox panel interpreted the midterm results as a warning that voters wanted relief from high costs, not another tariff program. Forbes said tariffs were one factor in voters turning against Trump, while other panelists emphasized that the public recognizes them as taxes. The cited Fox News poll—63 percent saying tariffs had harmed them financially—helps explain why a reliably conservative business program responded with disbelief rather than applause.

That does not establish that tariffs alone determined the election. It does establish a direct political conflict the administration cannot plausibly attribute to muddled communication: voters report financial harm, retailers warn of pricing pressure, markets react to instability, and even Trump-friendly commentators call the policy an unpopular tax.

Yet the White House is expanding the regime. The misdirection is to treat the resulting costs as unfortunate turbulence in a struggle with China and other foreign governments. The decision belongs to the Trump administration. So does the choice to repeat it after the political warning, the business objections and the legal challenge described by the panel.

Forbes’s prediction that the policy could change again within a week was delivered as a joke, but it captured the practical verdict. The people imposing the tariffs retain the freedom to improvise. Everyone required to set a price, take out a loan or buy imported goods must live with the bill.

item.title: Trump official’s chilling threat revealed in court docs
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration used control over billions of dollars in federal grants to pressure Intel into surrendering roughly 10 percent of the company to the government, according to court records described by WIRED and reported by AlterNet. The threat came from Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro, who told Intel’s chief financial officer in August 2025 not to mistake the demand for a negotiation and warned that rejecting it would bring consequences he could not predict. Intel’s board approved the deal.

That is the “chilling threat” in the court documents: accept the administration’s terms, or face unspecified retaliation from a government with enormous influence over Intel’s financing, customers and regulatory environment. The ambiguity was part of its force.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Federal grants became leverage for a government stake

Under the agreement, Intel would receive $8.9 billion in federal grants it had already secured, largely through the CHIPS Act. In return, the government would obtain about 10 percent of Intel’s stock without paying separately for the shares.

Notes from Shapiro’s call indicate that President Donald Trump intended to announce the deal that Friday. A summary prepared for Intel’s board records Shapiro acknowledging that directors could refuse, while adding that rejection would have consequences he could not predict. He also urged the board to consider the value of having the administration on Intel’s side, including in the company’s relationships with customers.

That formulation paired an inducement with a warning: cooperation could purchase presidential favor, while refusal could invite an undefined response. The administration held the institutional power. Intel’s directors possessed the formal authority to vote, but they were making that decision under pressure from officials controlling the release of federal money and invoking the president’s influence over the company’s commercial interests.

Board minutes show that directors considered the arrangement less than ideal. They accepted it anyway.

Trump described the extraction as effortless

Trump later advertised precisely the feature that makes the deal troubling. He wrote on social media that the United States had “paid nothing for these Shares,” which he valued at approximately $11 billion. Discussing the stake afterward, he said: “I should’ve asked for more. It was so easy.”

Before the agreement, Trump had publicly demanded the resignation of Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan over Tan’s connections to China. Tan met Trump in the Oval Office on August 11 and promised to divest his China-based holdings. The sequence described in the reporting placed the company and its chief executive under direct presidential pressure before Intel surrendered a major equity stake.

A shareholder lawsuit brought by Richard Paisner alleges that Intel’s board “caved to the government’s extortion.” Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute, called the transaction “straight-up coercion.” Those are their characterizations, not established judicial findings. But they track the language attributed to Shapiro: this was supposedly not a negotiation, the president’s announcement was already being prepared, and resistance would carry unknowable consequences.

Intel disputes that account. Its attorneys argue in a motion to dismiss that genuine negotiations occurred and improved the terms for the company, including the immediate release of its grants. That defense may explain why directors accepted the arrangement. It does not erase the reported warning that refusal could provoke consequences or the administration’s use of money Intel had already been awarded as leverage for an ownership stake.

Industrial policy turned into presidential patronage

The CHIPS Act grants were meant to support semiconductor production. In this transaction, the administration reportedly converted their release into leverage for acquiring corporate equity—and presented presidential favor as an asset Intel should price into its decision.

That is not merely aggressive economic policy. It replaces predictable administration of federal programs with a patronage logic in which companies are encouraged to calculate the value of being “on the side” of the president. The foreseeable consequence is a market shaped not only by statutes, grants and regulations, but by executives’ willingness to accommodate demands delivered with warnings of unspecified retaliation.

The same pattern reportedly extended to Nvidia. Trump announced that he had “convinced” Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO after the board chair had said days earlier that it would not do so. The New York Times reported that Nvidia reached an agreement with the administration on a Sunday night following days of pressure from senior Trump officials. Paisner is separately seeking Nvidia’s internal records concerning an agreement to give the government a share of its China chip sales.

The available reporting does not establish the merits of Paisner’s lawsuits or prove that either company’s directors violated their duties. It does show an administration using concentrated federal power to intervene in corporate governance, financing and sales—and a president publicly boasting about how little resistance he encountered.

Intel’s board could technically say no. Shapiro’s reported message explained why that freedom might be largely ceremonial: the people demanding the stake also claimed the power to make refusal hurt.

item.title: This is only the start of the greatest scandal of our lives
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump reportedly intervened to restore Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s chief executive after Huang was removed over an alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese operative. item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump reportedly intervened to restore Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s chief executive after Huang was removed over an alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese operative. According to AlterNet’s account of reporting by The New York Times and Reuters, Trump pressed Nvidia’s board to reverse its decision, privately assured directors that Huang would not face a criminal investigation, and acted despite intelligence warnings that the relationship posed a security risk. The episode, if accurately described, is not merely a corporate scandal. It is an alleged use of presidential power to influence a public company’s leadership, control the threat of prosecution and protect financial interests from which Trump himself stood to benefit.

AlterNet calls it the beginning of “the greatest scandal of our lives.” The supplied reporting cannot establish that superlative or prove several of its most serious inferences. It does, however, describe a concrete and extraordinary structure of power: the president signaling that legal exposure may depend on whether a corporation obeys him.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A board decision made under presidential pressure

Nvidia’s directors had unanimously removed Huang and opened an internal investigation, AlterNet reports, after learning of his relationship with Alice Huang, who is described as an operative for the Chinese Communist Party but is not related to him. The article alleges that her access helped advanced Nvidia technology reach China’s military. Reuters had also reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission opened an investigation.

Trump then called into an Nvidia board meeting and “reassured” directors that Huang was not a national-security threat and would not face criminal investigation, according to the account attributed to The New York Times. The board unanimously reinstated him.

That sequence makes the administration’s assurance look less like an independent assessment than leverage. Nvidia had already judged Huang sufficiently dangerous to remove him. Trump reportedly offered directors protection from federal scrutiny if they reversed course. Even without an explicit threat, a president discussing prosecution while demanding a personnel decision leaves a publicly traded company little room to treat the conversation as advice.

Trump’s own public argument further undermined his supposed reassurance. He warned that Huang might leave for China if Nvidia did not take him back. That claim casts Huang as valuable enough to Beijing that his departure could matter—hardly an obvious reason to dismiss the security concerns surrounding him.

Xi’s access and Washington’s secrecy

Trump reportedly discussed Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping before promising to do “whatever he could” to secure Huang’s return. AlterNet says Vice President JD Vance participated in conversations involving Huang and Nvidia, while awareness inside the government was confined to a small circle of senior officials.

The article further reports that Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth knew Alice Huang was suspected of spying before her relationship with Jensen Huang became public. If so, the administration was not scrambling to understand a newly revealed problem. Its most powerful officials allegedly knew the risk and proceeded anyway.

AlterNet goes further, suggesting Xi asked Trump to intervene and that Jensen Huang may have knowingly cooperated with Chinese interests. The supplied material does not establish either proposition as fact. Nor does it prove its speculation that recent technology outages were connected to China. Those remain attributed suspicions, not demonstrated findings.

The substantiated political question within the account is narrower and damning enough: why did the president insert himself into a corporate investigation involving alleged espionage after discussing the executive at issue with the leader of the country said to have benefited?

The president’s financial stake

AlterNet reports that Trump traded $100 million in Nvidia stock, that Huang contributed $25 million to Trump’s ballroom project and that the administration approved an arrangement allowing Nvidia chip sales to China in exchange for a share of revenue. It attributes that deal to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and separately alleges that Lutnick paid $25 million to retain his position after scrutiny of his connection to Jeffrey Epstein.

Those claims require careful attribution; the article does not establish bribery through a quoted finding or adjudication. But the reported financial overlap is central, not incidental. A president with Nvidia holdings allegedly used governmental authority to improve the position of Nvidia’s ousted chief. Nvidia’s share price then rose 31 percent, recovering more than $1 trillion in value lost the previous day. AlterNet, citing Judd Legum, calculates that the rebound increased the value of Trump’s holdings by $15 million.

That does not by itself prove that personal profit motivated Trump’s intervention. It does establish the conflict: Trump reportedly exercised public power in a matter capable of enriching him directly. His administration’s actions cannot be separated from that interest merely because the president also invoked national security—especially when his intervention overrode officials’ reported security concerns.

Enforcement as a loyalty benefit

The most consequential element is not the predictable hypocrisy of a Republican president dictating a private company’s leadership while his party denounces state control. “Communism” is an imprecise label for the conduct described here. The sharper description is personalized executive coercion: government benefits and legal protection allegedly distributed according to obedience and access.

Nvidia’s board may have welcomed Huang’s return, feared retaliation or calculated that submission was best for shareholders. The reporting does not resolve its motive. But directors were deciding under conditions Trump himself allegedly created. They had been told by the president that reinstatement would come with protection from investigation. Corporate independence becomes largely fictional when the White House can pair a preferred outcome with an assurance about whether federal law will be enforced.

That arrangement also turns national security into a bargaining chip. The alleged transfer of advanced technology to China’s military should have produced a process insulated from the president’s investments and relationships. Instead, the account depicts Trump deciding that Huang was safe, warning that he could defect to China and using prosecutorial discretion to obtain his reinstatement.

Congress inherits the unanswered questions

The political backlash described by AlterNet comes after a 2026 midterm election in which Republicans reportedly suffered defeats amid voter anger over affordability, accountability, artificial intelligence and the data centers supporting it. Oklahoma City Mayor David Holt, a Republican, said voters had rejected a party that had become “fringe” and “unworthy of governance.”

Some Republicans recognized the liability without confronting the power behind it. Senator Kevin Cramer raised the legal and reputational danger of employing a chief executive who could face espionage or export-control charges. That frames the problem as Nvidia’s hiring risk, when the more serious allegation is that the president tried to determine both the hiring outcome and whether the law would reach the person being hired.

Incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries promised a “swift, thorough and wide ranging investigation” into Nvidia’s conduct and Lutnick’s alleged abuse of power, saying Congress would examine whether the administration traded national security for personal gain. An investigation could establish which officials knew what, what Trump told Nvidia’s directors, whether enforcement decisions were offered conditionally and how the president’s financial interests were handled.

Until then, calling this the greatest scandal of anyone’s lifetime outruns the available facts. The reported conduct needs no inflation. A president allegedly intervened in a company’s boardroom, offered assurances about federal prosecution, disregarded intelligence warnings, acted after speaking with Xi and profited when the company’s value rebounded. The unresolved question is not whether that arrangement looked improper. It is how much of the federal government Trump used to make it happen.

item.content:encoded:
Charles Gasparino, a senior correspondent at Fox Business, argued Wednesday that Republican leaders outside the White House should either rescue the GOP or build a replacement because President Donald Trump has become a political liability—and, more damningly, an increasingly irrelevant one. His evidence was not simply a temporary market selloff. It was the failure of Trump’s intervention in Nvidia’s leadership drama to produce a lasting rally, combined with midterm losses Gasparino attributed to voters’ exhaustion with the president.

The messenger matters. This is not an opposition strategist trying to manufacture a Republican crisis. It is a prominent figure on a network that has helped sustain Trump’s political dominance, warning that his hold over voters, markets and his own party is disintegrating.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A presidential intervention the market quickly discounted

Gasparino’s argument followed Trump’s unsuccessful attempt to bolster a plunging stock market by securing Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s chief executive. Stocks initially recovered some ground after news of Huang’s return, according to AlterNet’s account, but the rebound did not last. The market resumed falling Wednesday morning.

“So much for Trump and Huang saving the markets,” Gasparino wrote. He blamed a “long slide of weirdness” and enough bad White House policy decisions to matter, saying the public had rejected what the administration was offering.

That assessment cuts through the spectacle surrounding Trump’s involvement. A president inserting himself into the leadership of a major corporation is an extraordinary concentration of political and economic influence. Yet Gasparino’s reading was that investors no longer believed Trump could reliably shape the outcome. The intervention displayed power; the market response exposed its limits.

Gasparino considered—and rejected—a more dramatic interpretation that investors might be anticipating legal jeopardy, impeachment and a Senate conviction with Republican support. His preferred explanation was simpler: markets increasingly treat Trump as a nonfactor.

Republicans cannot outsource responsibility to “weirdness”

Gasparino urged what remains of the Republican leadership beyond the White House to prepare either a new party or a rescue of the existing one because, as he put it, “this ain’t ending well.” But that formulation also lets Republican officials pretend they are spectators at a collapse they spent years enabling.

Trump did not acquire control of the GOP by wandering into an empty building. Republican officeholders surrendered institutional authority, enforced loyalty to him and attached their electoral fortunes to his persona. If voters are now rejecting that association, the resulting losses belong not only to Trump but to the party leaders who made him the party’s organizing principle.

AlterNet framed Gasparino’s criticism largely around Trump’s “weirdness,” but his own remarks went further. He cited bad policy decisions, diminished governing capacity and electoral damage in seats that should have been safe for Republicans. Those are consequences of political choices, not matters of style.

Reducing the crisis to eccentric behavior risks laundering responsibility. “Weirdness” is an aesthetic diagnosis. Trump’s attempt to influence Nvidia’s management, his weakened ability to enact policy and the losses Gasparino tied to his presidency concern the use—and deterioration—of actual power.

The attention machine is failing

Gasparino also pointed to Trump’s manipulated image placing Huang’s head on the president’s body after the assassination attempt while holding a bra. Even that provocation, he argued, produced little more than a collective yawn.

His conclusion was that Trump “no longer holds the public imagination for either good or bad.” For a politician whose leverage has long depended on monopolizing attention, indifference can be more disabling than outrage. Condemnation still places Trump at the center of the story. A shrug does not.

Gasparino said the midterms offered electoral evidence of the same shift: Republicans lost safe seats because voters wanted distance from the man in the White House. That remains Gasparino’s interpretation, not a motive established for every voter. But it explains why his warning was directed at Republican leaders. If Trump can no longer generate enough loyalty, fear or fascination to protect the party, continued submission becomes harder to justify even on its own cynical terms.

Nvidia inherits the risk of Trump’s ownership theater

Gasparino ended by describing Trump as effectively Nvidia’s chief executive and board combined—a characterization of the president’s intervention, not the company’s formal governance. His point was that Nvidia shareholders now bear the risk of being tied to a president whom he believes Americans are rejecting.

That is the immediate consequence obscured by the talk of personality. Trump tried to put presidential weight behind a corporate leadership decision. The market briefly moved, then resumed its decline. Republican leaders, meanwhile, face a problem of their own making: they built a party around one man’s ability to command events, and a Fox Business correspondent is now telling them that markets and voters no longer believe the command performance.

item.title: Revenge: Trump enemy says crucial nomination 'dead' as time runs out
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: John Cornyn has blocked T. item.content:encoded:
John Cornyn has blocked T. Elliot Gaiser’s nomination to a federal judgeship in Texas, telling MS NOW that the nomination is “not going anywhere.” The retiring Republican senator withdrew the home-state approval needed to advance Gaiser, frustrating the Trump administration’s attempt to fill the seat before Democrats take control of it. What AlterNet framed as revenge is more concretely an exercise of Senate power by a lawmaker whom Donald Trump can no longer punish politically.

A rushed nomination meets a Senate veto

Gaiser reportedly entered consideration only after Republicans suffered an overwhelming defeat in the midterm election. According to MS NOW, staff for Texas Sen. Ted Cruz first contacted him about a possible nomination on Nov. 4. Cornyn objected both to the compressed process and to Gaiser’s lack of meaningful ties to Texas.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

He then revoked his “blue slip,” the Senate Judiciary Committee’s mechanism for securing approval from both senators representing a judicial nominee’s state. That decision effectively halted the nomination. Cornyn told people close to him that Gaiser was “dead” for the time being, MS NOW reported, though neither the White House nor Senate websites indicated that the nomination had formally been withdrawn.

Trump’s allies expected Cornyn to surrender. Mike Davis, a longtime Trump legal adviser, presented the choice as accepting the administration’s nominee or handing the seat to Democrats: “You can have a very good nominee now, who may not be your top choice, or the Democrats are going to take the seats.”

That argument reveals the administration’s governing premise. The urgency was not principally about Gaiser’s qualifications or a careful search for a judge rooted in the state. It was about controlling a lifetime appointment before the political window closed.

Trump’s leverage expired with Cornyn’s career

Cornyn is scheduled to leave office early next year after losing his Republican primary. Trump backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a loyal MAGA figure, against him. Paxton’s scandal-heavy record and deep unpopularity were then widely credited with helping Democrat James Talarico capture the seat during the midterm wave.

Trump therefore succeeded in removing a Republican who crossed him, only to help produce a Democratic successor and liberate Cornyn from the pressure that once made presidential retaliation effective. With no reelection campaign left to threaten, Cornyn has resisted Trump’s legislative priorities and nominations.

Calling the Gaiser blockade “revenge” supplies a tidy personal drama, but it also obscures the institutional mechanics. Cornyn did not merely nurse a grievance; he used a prerogative available to a sitting senator. Trump and his allies had counted on party discipline, electoral intimidation and the fear of Democratic control to overcome Cornyn’s objections. That calculation failed because they had already stripped him of the incentive to comply.

None of this makes Cornyn an insurgent against partisan court-packing. His objection concerns the nominee and the process, not the Republican project of securing the seat. He is already urging Trump to nominate another conservative candidate quickly.

A replacement, if the clock allows

The administration has begun vetting Steve Fahey, a Cornyn-approved prospect with Texas ties, according to MS NOW. Cornyn described Fahey as “a highly accomplished prosecutor” who earned “stellar reviews” from the Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee and called on Trump to nominate him swiftly.

The remaining obstacle is time. It was unclear from the reporting whether Fahey could be nominated and confirmed before Jan. 3. Gaiser’s nomination had not officially ended, but Cornyn’s refusal left it without a viable path while the administration pursued an alternative.

The episode is less a principled break than a collision among competing forms of Republican power: Trump’s control over party careers, senators’ control over home-state judicial nominations and the approaching transfer of a seat to a Democrat. Trump used the first power to drive Cornyn out. Cornyn is now using the second to deny Trump his preferred nominee. The third may leave both men without the judgeship they were racing to secure.

item.title: Bombshell report reveals Trump’s conversations with Nvidia board members
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance privately engaged with Nvidia board members and lawyers over Jensen Huang’s reinstatement and participation in a presidential trip to China, while officials responsible for intelligence and export policy were reportedly excluded. CBS News reported that CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick did not know what was unfolding. Secretary of State Marco Rubio—who had personally warned Trump about intelligence concerning Huang’s relationships in China—was reportedly furious.

The significance is not merely that corporate representatives had the president’s ear. It is that their access appears to have overridden the administration’s own national-security process, leaving senior officials uninformed and producing a decision the attorney general could not—or would not—explain.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Rubio’s warning lost to a last-minute reversal

According to CBS News, Rubio prepared a classified memorandum earlier in the year based on U.S. intelligence, including intercepted conversations involving Alice Huang. The memorandum warned that Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who was known to communicate with an officer in China’s Ministry of State Security.

Rubio was also reportedly one of two officials who briefed Trump about Huang’s relationship with a Chinese spy. That concern initially kept Huang off the guest list for the China trip. But while Air Force One was refueling in Alaska, Trump added him at the last minute—even after Rubio personally explained why he considered it unsafe to include Huang on the diplomatic mission.

CBS reported that Nvidia told Trump and Vance late Sunday that Huang would be brought back on. One official described the message as a command, not a consultation: “We were told, ‘This is going to happen.’”

That sequence clarifies where the institutional power sat. Intelligence officials could collect information, the secretary of state could prepare a classified warning, and national-security officials could recommend excluding Huang. Trump could erase all of it with a last-minute decision after private discussions involving Nvidia.

Nvidia cited government approval the government could not explain

Nvidia said Monday that its board had received input “from senior levels of the United States government” and was confident Huang’s reinstatement presented no national-security risk. The statement did not reconcile that assurance with Rubio’s reported warning or the exclusion of Ratcliffe and Lutnick from the discussions.

Trump then offered a different and deeply muddled account during a call to CNBC. Asked what the attorney general had told him about Huang’s possible criminal exposure and export-control issues, Trump said an unspecified “they” had conducted a study and “pretty good investigation” that left Huang “exonerated.”

He then shifted to Nvidia’s chip sales, saying Huang could sell older products—apparently referring to “the 200s”—but not Blackwell chips or other advanced technology. Trump suggested future problems might arise if buyers resold Nvidia products, concluding, “Who knows.”

That was not an explanation of who investigated Huang, what conduct was examined, what legal standard applied, or how the reported national-security concerns had been resolved. It was presidential absolution without an identifiable process.

Attorney General Todd Blanche further undermined Trump’s account the following day. When reporters asked about an investigation, Blanche said he did not know what they were talking about and noted that the Justice Department handles hundreds or more export investigations at any given time. Asked specifically whether the Justice Department or FBI had investigated Huang as a security risk, Blanche responded: “What does that mean, for what? I don’t understand the question.”

Trump claimed an investigation had exonerated Huang. His attorney general professed ignorance of it. Nvidia claimed senior government input had eliminated the national-security concern. Senior officials responsible for intelligence and commerce were reportedly outside the conversation. Those accounts do not describe a functioning review; they describe a decision acquiring official justification after the people with direct access had already made it.

Export enforcement and corporate access

The surrounding financial interests make that exclusion more consequential. AlterNet, citing the CBS report, noted that Lutnick’s former company holds significant Nvidia investments, raising questions about his refusal to enforce export requirements involving the company. The supplied reporting does not establish why he declined to act, but it places the administration’s export-control decisions inside a web of corporate access and unresolved conflicts.

Nor has the wider scrutiny disappeared. CBS reporter Jennifer Jacobs said the FBI and the Justice Department’s National Security Division were examining potential export-control violations involving Megaspeed and Super Micro Computer, including who knew what and when. That report concerns ongoing scrutiny, not a finding of wrongdoing by Huang.

The central failure is already visible without prejudging those inquiries. Rubio’s warning reportedly reached Trump. Trump nevertheless reversed the security-based exclusion. Nvidia’s representatives had access to Trump and Vance while key officials remained unaware, and the administration subsequently produced incompatible stories about the review supposedly supporting its decision.

The “bombshell” is therefore not simply that Trump spoke with Nvidia’s board. Presidents routinely hear from corporate executives. It is that private corporate access appears to have displaced the government’s own security apparatus—and that when officials were asked to account for the result, the president invoked an exoneration his attorney general could not identify.

item.title: Trump staged a 'four-alarm' panic moment that no one noticed
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump used a summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin to sketch a world order in which the United States, China and Russia would police nuclear power while weakening the institutions and alliances that constrain them. item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump used a summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin to sketch a world order in which the United States, China and Russia would police nuclear power while weakening the institutions and alliances that constrain them. The alarming moment, according to Bulwark commentator Jonathan V. Last, was Trump’s announcement of a “Declaration toward Peace” that would enlist Washington alongside Beijing and Moscow to prevent other countries from developing nuclear deterrents—even as the United States begins pulling back from regions those countries depend on it to defend.

That is the “four-alarm” development obscured by complaints that the trilateral meeting produced little of consequence. If Last’s reading of Trump’s announcement is correct, the summit was not empty diplomacy. It was a statement of hierarchy: three nuclear powers claiming broad freedom of action while denying less powerful states the means to protect themselves.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A peace declaration built around concentrated power

At Trump’s Friday press conference after the summit, he said the three leaders had agreed to a “Declaration toward Peace.” Last identified four elements: restructuring the United Nations through cooperation among the three powers; increasing their oil production; resisting and discrediting the International Criminal Court; and working together to prevent nuclear proliferation.

The label does substantial political work. “Peace” suggests restraint, mutual security and reduced conflict. The reported substance instead combines control over energy, hostility toward an international accountability institution and cooperation among three powerful states to limit which other countries may possess nuclear weapons.

Preventing proliferation is not inherently sinister. The decisive question is who provides security to states persuaded—or pressured—not to build their own deterrents. Last argues that Trump is simultaneously accelerating American disengagement from Europe, the Middle East and the Pacific. Under that arrangement, allied countries would lose confidence in Washington’s protection while Washington joined Russia and China in restricting their alternatives.

The contradiction is not a technical defect. It is the mechanism through which power would be concentrated. A government that withdraws protection and then blocks self-protection is not practicing isolationism. It is asserting control without accepting the obligations that once accompanied American leadership.

“America First” turns outward

Last’s central argument is that the summit punctured the familiar description of “America First” as a retreat from foreign entanglements. The vision he describes is not a United States leaving other countries alone. It is a United States cooperating with two authoritarian governments to establish a three-power order over weaker states, including liberal democracies Washington previously treated as allies.

That distinction matters because “isolationism” can misdirect responsibility. It portrays the damage as absence: America steps away, a vacuum appears, instability follows. But the policy Last describes is active. Trump would not merely erode the security arrangements that have discouraged allies from acquiring nuclear weapons. He would then work with the governments those arrangements helped deter to prevent exposed countries from building deterrents of their own.

Last named Poland, Ukraine, Germany, Japan, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and Canada among the states that could feel compelled to seek nuclear weapons, while Britain, France and India could decide to expand their existing arsenals. That is his forecast, not a reported decision by those governments. But it follows from the security dilemma he identifies: assurances lose value when the country supplying them openly contemplates disengagement.

Russia’s place in the proposed hierarchy is especially revealing. As Last noted, its limited economic weight would not ordinarily justify treating it as one of three managers of the international system. Its military power and nuclear arsenal would. The arrangement would therefore reward coercive capacity, not democratic legitimacy, economic strength or adherence to international rules.

Accountability is also on the chopping block

The reported opposition to the International Criminal Court belongs in the same structure. Nuclear privilege protects the dominant states from military challenge; delegitimizing an accountability institution weakens another potential constraint on state conduct. Reforming the United Nations in concert with Russia and China would likewise give the three governments an opportunity to reshape multilateral authority around their shared interests.

The source material does not provide the declaration’s full text or establish how its provisions would be implemented. Trump’s announcement, as described by Last, nevertheless supplies the political direction: cooperation with Moscow and Beijing, reduced reliance on existing institutions, and a narrower circle of states entitled to decisive power.

That is why dismissing the summit as inconsequential misses the news. The absence of a conventional agreement does not make a presidential declaration meaningless. Presidents use alliances, recognition and public commitments to define what conduct their governments will tolerate and whose security they consider expendable.

Last once expected nuclear proliferation to be Trump’s lasting consequence because dismantling American alliances would push frightened states toward military expansion. After the summit, he reached a harsher conclusion: Trump was proposing to help create that insecurity and then align with Xi and Putin against the countries responding to it.

The distinction is between negligence and domination. On the facts Last reported, Trump did not simply fail to reassure allies. He described a system in which three great powers would reserve strategic autonomy for themselves while deciding how much defensive capacity everyone else could possess. “Peace” is the sales language. Dependency is the reported design.

item.title: The only way to end this national emergency
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: D. Earl Stephens’s answer to America’s purported “national emergency” is the immediate removal of President Donald Trump. Writing for AlterNet, he calls for sustained public pressure, including mass demonstrations in Washington, and demands that Democrats and major news organizations make Trump’s departure the central political question. But his culminating phrase — “by any means possible” — is recklessly undefined. The concrete measures he actually names are political: resignation, removal and
item.content:encoded:
D. Earl Stephens’s answer to America’s purported “national emergency” is the immediate removal of President Donald Trump. Writing for AlterNet, he calls for sustained public pressure, including mass demonstrations in Washington, and demands that Democrats and major news organizations make Trump’s departure the central political question. But his culminating phrase — “by any means possible” — is recklessly undefined. The concrete measures he actually names are political: resignation, removal and public mobilization.

Stephens’s argument is less a news report than an alarmed polemic built around a recognizable institutional problem: removing Cabinet officials would leave the president’s power intact, while congressional Republicans, in his account, have no intention of restraining him. The article accuses Trump of self-dealing, weaponizing the Justice Department, escalating immigration enforcement and surrounding himself with extremists. It offers those claims as the case for removal, though it frequently substitutes invective for the precise accounting that such a grave case requires.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Personnel changes would leave the machinery intact

Stephens rejects the idea that impeaching officials such as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. would resolve the crisis he describes. Trump, he argues, could consult Stephen Miller, install harsher replacements in acting roles and continue the same program.

That is the article’s strongest structural point. Cabinet officials exercise enormous authority, but the president selects them and sets the administration’s direction. Treating individual subordinates as isolated aberrations can obscure the person who appointed them and the political coalition that keeps the administration functioning. Removing one official may limit particular damage; it does not, by itself, dismantle the governing project.

Stephens places responsibility squarely on Republican lawmakers, whom he portrays as active enablers rather than helpless spectators. He singles out Marco Rubio as a politician who, in Stephens’s view, understands what Trump is doing but remains loyal because he imagines a future presidential nomination. Whether or not that motive can be established from the article, the institutional relationship is clear: Republican officials possess power they could use against the administration and, as Stephens tells it, are choosing accommodation.

Normal coverage can normalize abnormal power

The second target is the press. Stephens condemns the incremental style of coverage that records one administration action after another without reaching a judgment about the governing pattern. He names The New York Times and PBS NewsHour, accusing them of presenting an escalating attack on Americans as a conventional sequence of daily developments.

The criticism identifies a real journalistic failure mode, but Stephens weakens it by demanding that “reputable” outlets call directly for Trump’s removal. Reporting does not become adequate only when a newsroom adopts his preferred conclusion. The more defensible demand is for journalism that identifies responsibility, tests allegations, explains how presidential authority is being used and refuses euphemisms that disguise coercion or corruption.

Stephens himself does not consistently meet that standard. He calls Trump treasonous, describes the administration in criminal terms and presents numerous serious allegations with little development in this column. His contempt is unmistakable; the evidentiary chain is often not. Precision matters most when the accusation is most severe.

An electoral rebuke is not removal

Stephens describes a “Bluenami” in the November 3 election: Democrats won a majority among those who voted, he says, while fewer than half of eligible voters participated. He attributes the scale of the result largely to economic pain, including high prices and gasoline costs, and argues that some Trump supporters either stayed home or voted Democratic.

That interpretation carries an uncomfortable implication. Stephens believes voters tolerated environmental damage, state violence and presidential misconduct until the consequences reached their wallets. But the article supplies no polling establishing why people voted as they did. His causal account should therefore be read as political interpretation, not a demonstrated finding.

Even on Stephens’s terms, the election created an interregnum rather than an immediate transfer of power: the outgoing Congress remained in office while the incoming one waited to take its seats. That gap is central to his urgency. A repudiated administration can still exercise presidential authority, and an electoral loss does not automatically remove a president before the end of a term.

Yet the article never cleanly explains which lawful removal mechanism could succeed, who would initiate it or whether the necessary votes exist. It mentions impeachment of Cabinet members only to dismiss it, calls for Trump to step down and proposes mass demonstrations. Those are materially different paths. Collapsing them into “any means possible” produces heat where the argument needs constitutional and political specificity.

Democrats cannot communicate their way around a power struggle

Stephens wants Democrats to “wield their power ruthlessly” and designate a prominent figure to explain the administration’s conduct every day. Better communication may help the public understand disparate abuses as parts of a governing pattern. It cannot substitute for identifying the power Democrats actually possess, the procedures available to them and the officials blocking action.

His demand that every prospective 2028 Democratic presidential candidate advocate immediate removal exposes a familiar institutional evasion: politicians can turn a present crisis into campaign material for an election years away. But a loyalty test is not a removal strategy. If Trump’s continuation in office is the emergency Stephens describes, then speeches about 2028 are beside the point unless they are tied to action now.

The article’s answer is therefore morally emphatic but operationally incomplete. Stephens says Trump must leave; Republicans will not force him out; replacing subordinates will not suffice; the press is failing to describe the stakes; and public demonstrations should demand resignation. What he does not establish is how those ingredients produce removal.

That omission cannot be repaired with more extravagant language. A president is not displaced by the intensity of a columnist’s certainty. He is removed through specific institutions controlled by identifiable people — or persuaded to resign by political pressure strong enough to make remaining untenable. Stephens correctly directs attention toward those with power, then ends without specifying how that power would be compelled.
