item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration delayed the second round of awards from a $50 billion rural health fund, then changed what states would receive without explaining why. Eighteen congressional Democrats are now demanding that Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz disclose how the money is calculated, where it is going and whether rural hospitals—or consultants and technology firms—are actually receiving it.

The nine-day delay is consequential because the program is not merely a grant initiative. Republicans created it as a temporary cushion after President Donald Trump’s budget law imposed an estimated $137 billion in Medicaid cuts affecting rural America over 10 years. States are being asked to plan around a five-year fund while absorbing much larger, longer-lasting losses engineered by the same government.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A deadline missed, an explanation withheld

CMS was supposed to announce the second-year awards by Oct. 31. One day before that deadline, the agency told states it had discovered “an additional administrative process requirement.” It did not announce the allocations until Nov. 9.

The resulting changes were generally small in percentage terms, but states are operating health systems in which small shifts can carry immediate consequences. Illinois received roughly $3 million less than its first-year award of $193.4 million, a reduction of about 1.5%. Alabama lost $4.1 million, while Colorado’s allocation fell by nearly $3 million.

Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski said CMS gave the state no reason for its reduction and no information about an appeals process. She joined Alabama Rep. Terri Sewell and Colorado Sen. Michael Bennet in leading the letter to Oz, which requests answers by Nov. 25 and a briefing on the delay and its effects.

“Those kind of delays prevent a state to fully prepare for what’s to come,” Budzinski said.

That is the immediate administrative failure: CMS controls the scoring, the schedule and the flow of funds, while states and rural providers bear the consequences of unexplained changes. The agency has published data maps, press releases and presentations about its scoring system. Yet Alan Morgan, CEO of the National Rural Health Association, said the method still needs to be explained clearly enough that every state can understand and reproduce success.

CMS officials did not respond to AlterNet’s questions before its deadline.

Temporary relief for damage Congress created

The Rural Health Transformation Program distributes $10 billion annually for five years. First-year awards ranged from $147 million to $281 million, with all 50 states receiving money through a federal scoring process. Allocations are reconsidered each year; most moved by less than 2% in the second round. North Dakota and Iowa posted the largest gains, while New Jersey, Florida and Vermont sustained the largest reductions.

Those figures can make the program look like a substantial federal commitment. The political arithmetic says otherwise. Republicans added the fund to their budget legislation as a last-minute inducement while advancing Medicaid cuts that hit rural hospitals and patients especially hard. The temporary program amounts to less than half the estimated decade-long Medicaid reduction for rural America—and it expires after five years.

Cara James, president and CEO of Grantmakers in Health, called the fund “retail therapy for Congress” at a Milken Institute event. Her description identifies the misdirection built into the policy: lawmakers can advertise a new rural health program while the same law removes far more support from Medicaid, food assistance and other grants on which rural communities depend.

A short-term, competitively scored fund does not replace a durable insurance program. Medicaid payments sustain routine operations and care for patients; transformation grants arrive through administrative contests, shifting formulas and annual federal review. The former supports the financial base of rural care. The latter leaves states competing for partial relief from a crisis federal policy is deepening.

The money trail remains obscured

The lawmakers’ concern extends beyond how CMS divides money among states. They want to know who ultimately receives it.

Their letter warns that too much could flow to large consulting and technology companies instead of hospitals, clinics and communities. Budzinski said the point is to ensure that the money reaches rural providers rather than consultants. Democrats asked CMS to create a searchable spending database and explain how it will evaluate state performance and set future awards.

Morgan said his association’s analysis indicates that states are directing federal money to local hospitals and clinics. But he also said the overall division between frontline providers and other recipients, including consultants, remains unclear. That distinction matters because the program’s branding does not guarantee its beneficiaries. A dollar classified as rural health spending may finance a hospital’s care, or it may purchase planning, software and professional services several steps removed from a patient.

The administration created an Office of Rural Health Transformation to oversee the initiative. What it has not provided is the basic public accounting needed to judge whether “transformation” means keeping facilities open or building an administrative industry around their precarity.

State governments were initially given just over seven weeks to prepare applications for the first awards. They had to compete under a complicated scoring system, then accept annual revisions whose logic remains insufficiently clear to the officials affected. That arrangement concentrates discretion at CMS while dispersing responsibility downward: federal officials set the rules, but states and providers must explain service losses when the numbers change.

Hospitals are closing while Washington trades letters

Five rural hospitals have closed or converted to lower-level facilities since the program was established, according to a list maintained by the Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research at the University of North Carolina. One Michigan facility eliminated inpatient beds and shifted to emergency-only care in an effort to survive.

The fund has therefore not stopped the contraction it was presented as addressing. Nor could a temporary grant pool plausibly neutralize every effect of much larger Medicaid reductions. The unresolved issue is whether the program is at least delivering its limited resources efficiently and transparently.

Congress has asked before. Democrats wrote to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. about the rollout in August 2025, one month after the law passed. Budzinski later contacted Oz on Illinois’ behalf. Bennet, Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and other senators asked in June that the money be aimed at rescuing rural hospitals and clinics.

“We haven’t gotten full responses to any of these inquiries,” Budzinski said.

That repeated silence is not a communications problem for states to solve. Oz runs the agency that controls the awards. CMS can disclose its calculations, provide an appeals process and show where the money lands. Until it does, the administration is asking rural communities to trust a shifting formula attached to a temporary program created to soften the political impact of far larger cuts.

item.title: The 90-year-old forgotten weapon Dems can use right now to stop 'Mr. Veto'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The weapon is Congress’s inherent contempt power: the authority to direct its sergeant-at-arms to detain a witness who defies a congressional subpoena. item.content:encoded:
The weapon is Congress’s inherent contempt power: the authority to direct its sergeant-at-arms to detain a witness who defies a congressional subpoena. According to AlterNet, Democrats could revive that power—unused for roughly 90 years—when the new Congress convenes January 3. It would not neutralize President Donald Trump’s veto, but it could prevent his administration from turning congressional oversight into a request that executive officials may ignore without consequence.

That distinction matters. Trump may call himself “Mr. Veto,” and Democrats reportedly lack the two-thirds majorities needed to override him. But a presidential veto applies to legislation. It does not cancel hearings, approve judicial nominees or give the executive branch lawful authority to spend money Congress has not appropriated. The central question is therefore not whether Democrats possess institutional power. It is whether they will use the power voters have given them.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The administration is preparing to obstruct oversight

The incoming Congress is already confronting an administration that has signaled resistance to scrutiny. Asked whether the White House would comply with congressional subpoenas, White House counsel William Scharf answered, “it depends.” AlterNet also reports that Trump ordered federal agencies to obtain his personal permission before officials testify and that the Justice Department instructed U.S. attorneys to adopt a “wartime” posture toward Democratic demands for information, including requests involving the Epstein files.

Those are not ordinary disagreements over legislative priorities. They describe an executive branch attempting to decide for itself whether another branch of government may investigate it. If Congress accepts that arrangement, subpoenas become stationery and oversight becomes theater.

Democrats know the failure mode. During Trump’s earlier administration, Attorney General Bill Barr and Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross refused to appear and testify before Congress. The Justice Department declined to prosecute them for criminal contempt. That history exposes the weakness of the conventional process: Congress cites an executive official for contempt, then asks the executive branch to enforce the citation against one of its own.

The administration’s answer can simply be no.

Congress does not need Trump’s prosecutors to defend Congress

Inherent contempt offers a way around that dependency. Rather than referring a defiant witness to the Justice Department, Congress could authorize its own sergeant-at-arms to make an arrest. AlterNet presents the mechanism as a dormant but available congressional power, contingent on Democratic leaders—including House leader Hakeem Jeffries and either Chuck Schumer or Chris Van Hollen—being willing to revive it.

That is the real answer to the headline’s promise. The 90-year-old weapon is not a clever procedural trick for overriding vetoes. It is a coercive enforcement authority Congress could use when witnesses refuse lawful demands for testimony or records.

Its revival would be extraordinary, and the article does not report that Democratic leaders have committed to it. Nor would it resolve every legal dispute over executive privilege or the scope of a subpoena. But it would change who bears the cost of obstruction. Under the familiar contempt-referral process, an administration can protect its officials by withholding prosecution. Under inherent contempt, Congress asserts its own authority rather than outsourcing enforcement to the people it is investigating.

That prospect also clarifies where responsibility lies. If Democratic committees issue subpoenas they have no intention of enforcing, Trump’s defiance will not be the only institutional failure. The administration will have chosen obstruction; congressional leaders will have chosen impotence.

“Mr. Veto” is a useful piece of misdirection

Trump’s chosen nickname exaggerates one presidential power while diverting attention from the powers Congress retains. Beginning January 3, AlterNet reports, Democrats will hold 56 Senate seats. That would give them control over whether Trump confirms another judge. Congress can conduct hearings, demand records and use appropriations to restrict what the executive branch may lawfully spend.

None of those authorities requires a veto-proof majority.

Framing the next two years solely around Trump’s veto invites learned helplessness: Democrats propose bills, Trump rejects them, and party leaders explain that arithmetic made resistance impossible. But legislation is only one arena of conflict. Confirmation, investigation, appropriations and contempt are separate instruments. Treating all congressional power as if it disappears beneath the veto pen would be political misdirection, whether performed by Trump or adopted as an excuse by Democrats.

The source article surrounds this procedural argument with sweeping claims about oligarchy, federal collapse, political violence and public despair. Some of those claims are asserted more broadly than this specific report can establish. They are not necessary to understand the immediate power struggle. The concrete issue is narrower and more revealing: an administration is signaling that compliance with congressional oversight may be optional, while the incoming congressional majority possesses tools it has long declined to use.

The test is enforcement, not rhetoric

Democrats are reportedly preparing preservation demands and subpoenas aimed at Trump officials, family members and associates. Those steps may create records and expose conduct. But a subpoena without credible enforcement is merely an invitation addressed to people who have already announced their hostility to being questioned.

The temptation for congressional leaders will be to substitute televised indignation for institutional confrontation—to hold hearings about noncompliance, denounce the missing witnesses and then blame a Trump-controlled Justice Department for refusing to act. That sequence would generate clips while preserving the administration’s practical immunity from oversight.

Inherent contempt would force a harder choice. Congress would have to specify who defied it, defend the legitimacy of its demand and accept responsibility for enforcing the order. The administration, in turn, would have to challenge Congress openly rather than hiding behind prosecutorial inaction.

The dormant power is therefore more than a historical curiosity. It is a measure of whether the incoming majority intends to govern as a coequal branch or perform opposition inside boundaries drawn by Trump. Democrats cannot prevent every veto. They can decide whether “Mr. Veto” also gets to become Mr. No-Testimony, Mr. No-Records and Mr. No-Consequences.

item.title: Trump a 'visible embarrassment' thanks to family and 'yes-men': former aide
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: John Ullyot, a former deputy assistant to President Donald Trump during his second term, says Trump has become a “visible embarrassment” as relatives trade on his name, appointees perform televised rituals of praise and the president diverts attention from his stated agenda. But Ullyot’s more important admission is that none of this happened around Trump. item.content:encoded:
John Ullyot, a former deputy assistant to President Donald Trump during his second term, says Trump has become a “visible embarrassment” as relatives trade on his name, appointees perform televised rituals of praise and the president diverts attention from his stated agenda. But Ullyot’s more important admission is that none of this happened around Trump. Trump selected the personnel, rewards the flattery and remains responsible for the administration they serve.

“Ultimately the buck stops with the President,” Ullyot told the New Yorker. That point cuts through his more forgiving claim that Trump “deserves better” from his staff. A president is not the powerless customer of his own White House. He appoints advisers, establishes incentives and decides whether unwelcome information is valuable or disloyal.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Government by applause line

Ullyot singled out Trump’s televised Cabinet meetings, where officials take turns praising the president and competing to make the praise more extravagant. “That’s not serious,” he said.

It is also more than an aesthetic embarrassment. Cabinet members oversee institutions with public responsibilities. When their appearances become demonstrations of personal allegiance, scrutiny gives way to performance. Officials learn that the safest report is the one the president wants to hear, while the cameras show everyone else what advancement requires.

Ullyot compared the atmosphere with former Ford CEO Alan Mulally’s approach to internal reporting. As Ullyot recounted it, executives initially marked every business unit green even while Ford was losing billions. When one executive finally presented a red slide, Mulally applauded him. The point was simple: leaders who punish bad news eventually stop receiving it.

Trump, Ullyot said, prefers good news. That preference creates an opening for sycophants, but it does not absolve the person who created the market for sycophancy. The “yes-men” framing risks treating presidential management as something inflicted on Trump by overeager subordinates. Ullyot ultimately rejected that escape route himself: Trump needs stronger advisers, he said, but Trump is responsible for surrounding himself with them.

The first-term mythology breaks down

Ullyot portrayed Trump’s first term as a period of sharper concentration on three campaign promises: ending “forever wars,” draining the swamp and putting America first. New Yorker writer Isaac Chotiner challenged that account, recalling Trump’s late-night tweeting, extensive television watching and golfing.

Ullyot conceded the point. Those habits, he acknowledged, had not changed. His narrower argument was that Trump had lost focus on implementing his promises during the second term and had become distracted by projects including his ballroom.

That exchange matters because it strips away a convenient story of decline from disciplined governance into present disorder. Even Ullyot’s defense required revision once confronted with Trump’s documented first-term conduct as Chotiner described it. The distinction Ullyot finally drew was not between an attentive president and an inattentive one, but between recurring personal habits and what he considers a worsening failure to pursue the agenda Trump advertised.

“Drain the swamp” is particularly hollow in Ullyot’s account. He told the New Yorker that former aides and Trump’s family were “cashing in on his name.” When Chotiner asked whether he blamed the family more than Trump, Ullyot answered, “Well, it’s his family.”

That identifies the participants without resolving responsibility. Trump’s relatives may benefit from the family name, but the political value of that name comes from Trump’s office and continuing power. Ullyot said Trump was reportedly surprised by some revelations. Surprise, if accurately reported, would not demonstrate that the president lacked authority. It would show that he failed to monitor conduct close enough to him to become what Ullyot called a public embarrassment.

The excuse collapses into the indictment

Ullyot’s criticism remains caught between loyalty and diagnosis. He repeatedly says Trump “deserves better,” language that casts the president as the disappointed victim of a defective organization. Yet every concrete detail he offers points back toward Trump: the preference for praise, the indulgence of televised adulation, the distractions, the failure to scrutinize his operation and the absence of a clear prohibition against relatives exploiting his name.

Ullyot said Trump should have set the tone at the beginning of his second term and declared, “No more of this B.S.” Instead, by Ullyot’s telling, Trump allowed a system in which subordinates flatter him, relatives embarrass him and inconvenient realities may struggle to reach him.

The former aide’s corporate analogy therefore lands harder than he appears to intend. A chief executive who receives only green slides while the enterprise deteriorates is not vindicated by his preference for green. He has built an information system designed to protect himself from the facts. In a presidency, the consequences do not remain inside a brand. The officials performing loyalty for Trump exercise public power, and the country—not the steward of that brand—absorbs the cost of decisions made inside the applause chamber.

item.title: Trump’s religion ambassador tells Fox it's time to ‘move on’ from MAGA
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Sam Brownback, the former Kansas governor and senator whom Donald Trump appointed as ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom, told Fox News on Friday that voters are “ready to move on past President Trump.” His assessment was not merely that Republicans suffered an ordinary midterm setback. item.content:encoded:
Sam Brownback, the former Kansas governor and senator whom Donald Trump appointed as ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom, told Fox News on Friday that voters are “ready to move on past President Trump.” His assessment was not merely that Republicans suffered an ordinary midterm setback. Brownback said the rejection “was really targeted at President Trump,” including opposition to an immigration crackdown voters regarded as “too mean and aggressive.”

That distinction matters because Brownback is not a Democratic critic translating an election into a partisan attack. He is a longtime Republican and former Trump appointee telling the president’s preferred television audience that MAGA’s defining political product—punishment presented as strength—has become an electoral liability.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Brownback punctures the routine excuse

Republicans have tried to soften their midterm defeat by noting that presidents commonly lose congressional seats. Brownback rejected that consolation. In his telling, voters were not simply following a familiar midterm pattern; they were repudiating Trump personally.

Brownback maintained that the backlash was not necessarily ideological, although his own examples were plainly connected to government policy. He cited anger over inflation and gasoline prices, which AlterNet linked to Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran. He also said some voters approved of a secured border while objecting to the administration’s deportation campaign as excessively harsh.

That is the political problem Trump’s defenders prefer to blur. Border policy and the manner in which state power is exercised are not separable when the administration has made aggressive enforcement central to its identity. Brownback’s formulation attempts to preserve the policy while conceding that its implementation repelled voters. Even so, it recognizes something the administration has repeatedly denied: cruelty is not merely a communications problem when officials deliberately make visible suffering part of the deterrent.

“People want America to be a force for positive and good,” Brownback said. “I think we’ve got to show people kindness.” He closed by invoking Trump’s “hubris and pride” and warning, “Pride comes before a fall and a haughty spirit before a stumble.”

Conservatives discover an expiration date

Brownback’s break is part of a broader retreat among conservatives described by AlterNet. Utah Gov. Spencer Cox said earlier in the week that Trump should “move on” because “it’s time for the next thing.” Conservative radio host Erick Erickson similarly warned Republicans after the midterms not to “double down on crazy.”

The language is revealingly evasive. “Move on” treats Trumpism like a television season that has run too long, not a political project enabled for years by Republican officeholders, donors, media personalities and celebrity validators. The people now announcing its expiration were not powerless spectators. They helped give Trump institutional control and cultural legitimacy. Their belated concern about tone and excess arrives after voters imposed a cost.

The retreat has spread beyond elected Republicans. Dana White, who spoke at all three Trump political conventions and remained close to him for a decade, told Lara Trump on Fox News, “You’ll never see me involved in politics. I want nothing to do with politics.” Elon Musk, after spending hundreds of millions of dollars supporting Trump and his allies and briefly leading DOGE in the administration, now claims he is “not MAGA.”

Neither statement erases the power already supplied. Money, access and public endorsement do not disappear when their providers rebrand themselves as detached observers. Abandonment after defeat is not accountability; it is an attempt to escape the consequences of an alliance that has become less useful.

Republican resistance arrives on the way out

Trump’s weakening position is also appearing inside Congress, particularly among Republicans who will not remain after the term ends. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky attempted to initiate the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis blocked several Trump nominees despite pressure from the White House to confirm them before Democrats assumed the congressional majority.

These actions suggest that Trump’s control over Republican lawmakers depended at least partly on their fear of what he could do to their careers. Once that leverage diminished, resistance became possible. That does not make the departing lawmakers courageous so much as it clarifies the structure of obedience: the president’s hold was enforced through political incentives, and some Republicans opposed him only when those incentives no longer applied.

Brownback’s Fox appearance carries the same unmistakable calculation. He framed the midterms as a personal rejection of Trump, identified the administration’s aggression as a liability and urged a kinder politics only after the electorate punished the party. The conservative establishment is not suddenly confused about what MAGA became. Its members are deciding, one by one, that they no longer want to be held responsible for it.

item.title: Trump’s Texas hatchet-man drops all cases at once in 'humiliating' retreat
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Ken Paxton’s final weeks as Texas attorney general have become an exercise in destroying the evidence of his office’s political priorities—not by concealing records, but by abandoning the cases that made those priorities unmistakable. After losing his bid for the U.S. Senate and his post in a Democratic sweep, Paxton abruptly withdrew a string of lawsuits targeting immigrant aid organizations, transgender athletes, a Muslim civil rights group and others. Some dismissals permanently bar the state
item.content:encoded:
Ken Paxton’s final weeks as Texas attorney general have become an exercise in destroying the evidence of his office’s political priorities—not by concealing records, but by abandoning the cases that made those priorities unmistakable. After losing his bid for the U.S. Senate and his post in a Democratic sweep, Paxton abruptly withdrew a string of lawsuits targeting immigrant aid organizations, transgender athletes, a Muslim civil rights group and others. Some dismissals permanently bar the state from reviving similar claims.

The retreat matters because these were not incidental disputes. Paxton used the authority and public funding of the attorney general’s office to turn conservative grievances into state litigation, often against organizations with far fewer resources than Texas. Now, before Democrat Nathan Johnson can inherit the cases and decide their fate, Paxton is disposing of them himself.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The state walks away after imposing the costs

Among the defendants was Annunciation House, an El Paso shelter for migrants led by Ruben Garcia. Paxton’s office accused the organization of harboring undocumented immigrants and participating in human smuggling. According to the Houston Chronicle, the state dropped the suit without explanation.

Garcia described the withdrawal as an immense relief, but the state’s exit does not restore what the litigation consumed. He said Annunciation House lost money to legal fees and lost donors while defending itself against Texas. State power extracted those costs even though the case never reached a judgment validating Paxton’s allegations.

“The case was very much alive,” Garcia said. “I can’t help but believe that this was an acknowledgement of the writing on the wall.”

Paxton’s office also abandoned a case against FIEL, a Houston-area immigrant advocacy group. The Annunciation House and FIEL cases were dismissed with prejudice, meaning the attorney general’s office surrendered its ability to bring similar charges against the organizations later. That choice goes beyond a temporary change in litigation strategy. It closes the door Paxton’s own office had insisted needed to remain open.

Former Maine Attorney General James Tierney, a Democrat, offered the blunt interpretation: “The lawsuits have no merit, and he knows it.” That is Tierney’s assessment, not a judicial finding. But the unexplained withdrawals give Paxton’s office responsibility for answering the obvious question it has so far left to others: If these cases justified deploying the state’s lawyers and money, why abandon them now?

A culture-war docket collapses at once

The immigrant organizations were not isolated beneficiaries of Paxton’s retreat. His office also stopped pursuing a lawsuit against the NCAA over transgender athletes and, according to the Chronicle, is no longer pursuing a case against the Council on American-Islamic Relations. It withdrew support for a MAGA-aligned doctor reprimanded for prescribing ivermectin during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The cases shared a political function even where their legal claims differed. Each placed the Texas attorney general’s office inside a national conservative conflict—immigration, transgender participation in sports, Muslim civil rights or pandemic-era medical backlash. Paxton had made that alignment a defining feature of his tenure, using the state’s institutional weight against targets already marked as enemies by the Trump movement.

Former Washington Attorney General Rob McKenna, a Republican, told the Chronicle that an outgoing attorney general abandoning cases on this scale was extraordinary. “It’s not at all normal,” he said. “I can’t think of another example of an AG doing that.”

That unusual concentration of dismissals makes the timing politically revealing, even if Paxton has not supplied a public explanation. Nathan Johnson is preparing to take control of the office and has said he will end its service as what he described as a publicly financed law firm for MAGA interests. Paxton’s withdrawals deny the incoming attorney general the chance to terminate the cases himself—and to expose, through that process, which arguments the new administration considers indefensible.

“My guess is they don’t want to grant me the privilege of terminating their bad work,” Johnson told Texas Monthly. “They don’t want me taking credit.”

It is an inference, but one grounded in the transfer of power unfolding around the dismissals. Paxton is not merely leaving office. He is clearing contested litigation from the desk before his successor can examine and repudiate it.

Texas supplied the lawyers; weaker targets paid the price

Under Paxton, Texas became an important launch site for conservative legal campaigns. His office defended the state’s severe abortion restrictions and an immigration law authorizing local police to arrest migrants, an authority traditionally exercised by the federal government. The U.S. Supreme Court allowed both measures to take effect.

That record shows why describing Paxton as merely a partisan provocateur understates his power. He controlled a state legal apparatus capable of burdening organizations with expensive litigation, defending coercive laws and advancing cases through conservative courts toward a Supreme Court often receptive to his arguments. His targets had to respond whether or not the cases ultimately survived. Annunciation House’s lost donations and legal expenses were not rhetorical fallout; they were material consequences imposed by the state.

The dismissals do not prove that every abandoned claim was knowingly frivolous when filed. They do, however, expose the asymmetry built into this kind of government litigation. Paxton’s office could initiate headline-generating confrontations at taxpayer expense. The organizations he targeted had to divert their own money and labor to survive them. When the political conditions changed, the state could simply walk away.

Johnson has called the arrangement corrupt, arguing that MAGA treated Texas as “their own private law firm” while the public paid the bill. His description identifies the central abuse alleged here: not that an attorney general pursued policies consistent with his politics, but that the office’s coercive and financial power was harnessed to a national movement’s chosen enemies.

Paxton’s final act does not erase that record. It sharpens it. Annunciation House and FIEL are protected from a renewed attack on similar grounds, but neither recovers what the state forced it to spend. Paxton leaves before his successor can fire him from cases that, at the decisive moment, Paxton was unwilling to defend himself.

item.title: Trump’s rambling presser torn to shreds as he insists 'I don’t ramble'

item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump returned from Asia on Friday and used a White House press conference to deliver more than 30 minutes of uninterrupted remarks without taking a single question. The president’s rebuttal to criticism of his speaking style supplied the event’s defining contradiction: “I don’t ramble. I don’t ramble at all,” he said, before moving through potholes, data centers, Russia, China and his party’s midterm defeat.

The disorder was not merely cosmetic. Trump used a presidential platform to evade scrutiny, repeat the falsehood that the 2020 election was stolen and recast Republican losses as evidence that other Republicans had failed him. The White House called a press conference; the president provided a monologue.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

An election defeat becomes somebody else’s fault

Trump repeatedly returned to the midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of both the House and Senate. “I wasn’t on the ballot. I hope you remember that,” he said.

That defense attempted to sever the president from his party’s defeat while preserving his authority over the party itself. Trump claimed voters believed Republicans had treated him poorly because “they didn’t get the things that I wanted passed.” The electorate, in this account, did not reject his leadership or its consequences. It punished congressional Republicans for insufficient obedience.

Trump also asserted that the “world is not happy about the people that did well in the election.” AlterNet did not report whom he meant by “the world,” leaving the claim as an insinuation rather than an identifiable argument. The vagueness serves a political function: defeat can be blamed on hostile forces without naming evidence that could be examined.

The institutional facts are less accommodating. Democrats’ control of Congress means Trump’s legislative power has narrowed. His response was to deny political ownership of the result and demand that Republicans interpret their losses as a failure to deliver his agenda.

The record intrudes on the sales pitch

Trump paired complaints about the election with boasts about the money he said he had brought into the United States. But the economic figure included in AlterNet’s report cuts against a simple victory narrative: annual inflation was 3.7 percent in September, up from 3 percent when Trump took office in January 2025, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The comparison does not by itself establish why inflation rose. It does establish that Trump’s self-congratulation occurred alongside a worsening of a major economic measure during the stated period.

The White House tried to give the trip a more concrete frame before Trump spoke, distributing a list of what it called “historic deals” reached with the Philippines and Thailand that week. The list included a $12 billion Philippine Airlines order for 20 Boeing 787 jets. That is a specific commercial agreement. Trump’s broader claims about national success were far less disciplined.

False history as presidential alibi

Trump again claimed the 2020 election was rigged and linked that false premise to Russia’s war in Ukraine. “Frankly, if the election weren’t rigged, where I had to wait four years, that would never have happened,” he said.

The assertion allowed Trump to combine two familiar forms of self-exoneration. First, his electoral loss becomes theft. Then a war launched by Russia becomes something that occurred only because he was improperly kept from power. Neither move addresses his campaign promise to end the war on his first day back in office, a promise that remained unfulfilled in the reporting.

Trump also advertised his relationships with Russian and Chinese leaders as proof of diplomatic competence. He repeatedly emphasized that Chinese President Xi Jinping had greeted him at the airport, calling it an unprecedented honor, and said, “I get along with Russia. I get along with China.”

Personal access is not a foreign policy outcome. Being greeted warmly by another head of state does not establish what concessions were obtained, whose interests were protected or whether the United States gained anything durable. Yet Trump returned to the ceremony because it placed him—not policy, institutions or measurable results—at the center of the story. He dismissed skeptics as “the stupid people, some of them in this room,” substituting insult for an account of what the relationship had produced.

Data centers get the power; communities get advice

Trump said his administration would “fight very hard for the data centers” and urged communities to accept the facilities while extracting payment from their developers. “Make them pay you. Make them pay your community, but take advantage. Don’t shut them off,” he said.

The formulation revealed the administration’s priority. Communities were told to negotiate compensation, but the federal government’s commitment was directed toward the industry. Trump warned that technology companies could build abroad instead, while threatening a “tremendous tax” if they did. He also promoted renaming artificial intelligence “super intelligence,” or “SI,” branding a technology debate whose material stakes include infrastructure, public resources and corporate power.

Even Trump’s pothole detour carried the same absence of governing substance. “When you fix a pothole, you have brand new asphalt against old white asphalt,” he observed. The remark arrived not as part of a detailed infrastructure proposal but as another fragment in a presidential performance insulated from follow-up.

That insulation was the event’s most consequential feature. Reporters were assembled, handed the administration’s preferred record of achievement and then denied any opportunity to question the president about it. Trump could blame Republicans, invoke a stolen election, claim credit for prosperity, elevate airport protocol into diplomacy and threaten taxes on overseas data-center construction without being pressed to reconcile one assertion with the next.

The rambling mattered because the White House made it unilateral. Trump did not merely speak incoherently while denying that he rambles. He used the authority of the presidency to replace examination with assertion—and then left without taking a question.

item.title: CNN supercut prompts reporter to ask how Trump nominees 'sleep at night'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump’s nominees could not plainly acknowledge that Joe Biden won the 2020 popular vote because the truth itself appeared politically disqualifying. In confirmation hearings reported by AlterNet, candidates for powerful oversight and security posts repeatedly substituted evasions for an elementary fact—apparently calculating that looking dishonest or incompetent before Congress was safer than contradicting the president who nominated them. A CNN compilation made the pattern difficult to d
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s nominees could not plainly acknowledge that Joe Biden won the 2020 popular vote because the truth itself appeared politically disqualifying. In confirmation hearings reported by AlterNet, candidates for powerful oversight and security posts repeatedly substituted evasions for an elementary fact—apparently calculating that looking dishonest or incompetent before Congress was safer than contradicting the president who nominated them.

A CNN compilation made the pattern difficult to dismiss as an isolated verbal stumble. Asked by Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut who won the 2020 popular vote, Michael LoSapio, Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, refused to answer “a question about an election six years ago.” Michael Chamberlain, nominated to direct the Office of Government Ethics, would say only that Biden “was the president for four years.” Education Department inspector general nominee Mark Priebe managed that Biden won the popular vote, then immediately retreated into the safer formulation that he “was certified to be the president.”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

These were not obscure historical questions. They were tests of whether officials entrusted with cybersecurity, ethics enforcement and independent oversight would state an established fact when doing so could anger the president.

Loyalty performed as incompetence

A CNN reporter described “certified” as an answer Trump nominees had “workshopped over time”—a way to avoid the response they believed could get them in trouble with Trump. That distinction matters. Certification language sounds procedural and bloodless; it acknowledges that Biden occupied the office without conceding the legitimacy of the voters’ decision.

The nominees’ clumsy performances therefore should not be mistaken for confusion. Each was responding to a clear incentive created by presidential power: Trump controlled the nomination, and fidelity to his false account of 2020 appeared to matter more than candor before the Senate. The evasions were humiliating, but they were rational inside an administration where acknowledging reality could threaten access to office.

That is why the CNN panelist’s question—how these nominees can “sleep at night” after looking so “ridiculous, absurd, and out of touch with reality”—captures the degradation but not the full institutional problem. Personal shame is a weak restraint when the political system offers authority as the reward for public abasement.

The offices involved make the exercise particularly revealing. CISA helps protect election infrastructure. The Office of Government Ethics is supposed to enforce standards inside the executive branch. Inspectors general are expected to investigate departments without bending to political convenience. Nominees seeking such posts were demonstrating, on the record, that they would distort a straightforward answer when honesty conflicted with Trump’s preferences.

The Senate’s belated limit

The strategy also appeared to be losing some of its effectiveness. The CNN reporter argued that Trump had entered a lame-duck phase and that nominees willing to sound like “complete idiots” were finding confirmation harder, even during the final days of a Republican Senate majority.

Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina supplied the clearest evidence of resistance. According to AlterNet, Tillis placed holds on two Trump nominees after one denied that an attack occurred at the Capitol on January 6, 2021. Tillis also questioned whether another nominee, closely tied to Trump, could remain objective while leading the Government Accountability Office.

That intervention is meaningful, but it should not be inflated into a Republican break with Trump. A hold on two nominees is a procedural obstacle, not a repudiation of the loyalty system that produced them. It shows that at least one Republican senator found the performances—or the risks attached to them—too severe to wave through. It does not erase the fact that nominees reached confirmation hearings after apparently concluding that reality itself had become negotiable.

The real confirmation test

Blumenthal’s questions exposed the unofficial qualification these nominees were trying to satisfy. The Senate was ostensibly evaluating professional competence and independence. Trump’s political order imposed a different test: whether an appointee would protect his account of the past even when the evasion was obvious, recorded and absurd.

That test turns confirmation hearings into demonstrations of obedience. The nominee does not merely avoid offending the president; he shows future subordinates, regulated institutions and investigators that plain facts can be subordinated to presidential grievance. For officials who may oversee elections, ethics rules and government accountability, that is not an embarrassing side issue. It is evidence about how they might use the office.

The most revealing answer came not from any nominee but from the pattern connecting them. Each understood the question. Each understood the factual answer. What they feared was the consequence of saying it.

item.title: GOP senator’s defection imperils Trump’s last-minute nomination spree
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump’s rush to install loyalists before Democrats take control of Congress in January hit an obstacle Thursday when Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said he would hold Michael LoSapio’s nomination to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The break came after LoSapio, a Palantir security executive, told senators he did not believe the January 6, 2021, assault on the Capitol was an attack. item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s rush to install loyalists before Democrats take control of Congress in January hit an obstacle Thursday when Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said he would hold Michael LoSapio’s nomination to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The break came after LoSapio, a Palantir security executive, told senators he did not believe the January 6, 2021, assault on the Capitol was an attack.

A hold does not automatically kill a nomination. But with the incoming Democratic majority narrowing the time available for confirmation, Tillis’s move—joined by Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden—makes LoSapio’s installation at CISA substantially less likely. One Republican’s refusal to cooperate has exposed how little margin Trump’s final confirmation drive has left.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A basic question, then a revealing refusal

LoSapio’s nomination foundered on a question that required neither specialized cybersecurity knowledge nor a partisan judgment.

“Was there an attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021?” Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked during Thursday’s testimony.

“I, I, I don’t know,” LoSapio initially answered. After further questioning, he settled on a denial: “No, I don’t believe it was an attack, no.”

Blumenthal paused before asking whether LoSapio was really giving that answer. The nominee then tried to relocate the matter outside his claimed area of competence: “I wasn’t involved in politics.”

“You weren’t involved in politics? Were you alive on the planet?” Blumenthal replied.

That exchange was not a dispute over terminology at the margins. Trump nominated LoSapio to run the federal agency responsible for cybersecurity and election security. A prospective CISA director who declines to recognize an assault on the constitutional transfer of power is not avoiding politics; he is adopting a politically useful description of an event central to the office’s mission.

Wyden made the objection explicit: “You can’t have an insurrectionist Palantir executive in charge of our nation’s cybersecurity and election security.”

Tillis did not publicly give a specific reason for his hold. But AlterNet reports that he informed Punchbowl News of the decision shortly after LoSapio’s January 6 testimony. The timing leaves the exchange as the reported catalyst without turning an inference into a stated explanation.

Trump’s confirmation machine loses a vote

Tillis’s intervention matters because Republicans are trying to confirm as many Trump nominees as possible before control of Congress changes. The pressure is institutional, not procedural trivia: confirmation would place Trump’s choices in powerful federal posts that outlast the frantic closing days in which the Senate approved them.

Tillis, who is retiring, has become more willing to resist MAGA positions as his departure approaches. That freedom is revealing. Republican senators facing continued dependence on Trump’s political apparatus have stronger incentives to accept nominees whose testimony would ordinarily invite rejection. Tillis’s looming exit reduces that leverage over him; it does not explain why comparable independence should require retirement.

His resistance also extends beyond LoSapio. On Thursday, Tillis placed a hold on Eric Ueland’s nomination to lead the Government Accountability Office. He raised concerns that Ueland, an Office of Management and Budget official with close ties to the Trump administration, could not objectively direct an institution charged with government accountability.

The two holds point to the same governing problem from different directions. Trump sought to put a loyal administration figure in charge of auditing government performance and a nominee unwilling to call January 6 an attack in charge of protecting election infrastructure. Tillis’s decisions interrupt that effort, but they also underscore how far it had already advanced: both men reached the stage where a single senator’s late objection became decisive.

Denial meets an agency already stripped down

LoSapio’s January 6 answer was not the only concern raised by his testimony. Opponents also questioned his approach to CISA’s staffing and budget. He argued that additional money or personnel would not necessarily produce “more security.”

As an abstract proposition, that is unobjectionable; spending alone does not guarantee capacity. In the circumstances AlterNet describes, however, it functions as a convenient evasion of the agency’s actual condition. CISA insiders said the agency has struggled since former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem oversaw the departure of thousands of employees. Remaining staff have warned that the country’s lead cyber-defense agency is under-resourced while a series of technology-system outages has disrupted the nation over the previous week.

That context makes LoSapio’s posture consequential. The nominee was not being asked to manage an agency bloated with unused capacity. He was seeking control of one reportedly depleted of thousands of workers while dismissing any straightforward connection between resources and security.

The nomination therefore joined two forms of denial: refusal to describe January 6 in plain language and reluctance to acknowledge the operational implications of a gutted cybersecurity workforce. Neither demonstrates the candor required to lead an agency whose value depends on recognizing threats before political convenience makes them impossible to name.

LoSapio may not be formally finished, and a Senate hold is not a rejection. But the administration’s last-minute timetable has converted delay into a serious barrier. Trump’s nomination spree depended on Republican compliance; Tillis withheld it, and the candidate’s own testimony supplied the reason other senators needed to stop pretending this was a routine appointment.

item.title: Top Republican comes out swinging against Trump Cabinet officials
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Sen. Tom Cotton says he warned President Donald Trump’s administration that U.S. artificial-intelligence chips were reaching China through Chinese Communist Party front companies—and that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick failed to respond adequately before the Nvidia controversy erupted. Cotton’s complaint is not merely that officials missed a foreseeable risk. It is that they received repeated warnings from the Republican chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee and acted too late, leaving t
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Tom Cotton says he warned President Donald Trump’s administration that U.S. artificial-intelligence chips were reaching China through Chinese Communist Party front companies—and that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick failed to respond adequately before the Nvidia controversy erupted. Cotton’s complaint is not merely that officials missed a foreseeable risk. It is that they received repeated warnings from the Republican chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee and acted too late, leaving the government to assess what he called “the damage that’s been done.”

The Arkansas Republican has not demanded Lutnick’s resignation. He has instead left that judgment to Trump, who has publicly defended his commerce secretary and said he does not plan to replace him. That distinction matters: Cotton is attacking the administration’s handling of China policy while preserving the president’s authority—and responsibility—to decide whether failure carries consequences.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Warnings met with inaction

Cotton told The Wall Street Journal that he sent Lutnick multiple letters about Chinese front companies and the risk of advanced American chips being smuggled into China.

“If Howard Lutnick wanted my support, perhaps he should have responded to my many letters warning about these Chinese communist front companies and, more importantly, taking the threats of communist China more seriously,” Cotton said.

His account places the Commerce Department at the center of the failure. The department had regulatory authority relevant to the reported chip transfers; Cotton says its leadership was repeatedly alerted to the danger. If that account is accurate, the administration cannot plausibly reduce the episode to an unforeseeable breach. The dispute is about whether officials with power to act discounted warnings until the consequences became politically impossible to ignore.

Cotton welcomed the administration’s eventual movement toward his harder line on China, singling out national-security adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as an official who shared that view. But he described the shift as badly delayed.

“I’m glad that some folks in the administration are finally coming around to a view that I have championed and that others in the administration have as well,” he said. “It’s just a bit late, regrettably, and I think we need to catalog the damage that’s been done.”

That demand is more consequential than the personnel drama. A serious accounting would identify what technology reportedly reached China, which companies or intermediaries moved it, what warnings officials received, and which decisions allowed the transfers to continue. Cotton’s remarks, as reported, do not provide that inventory. They establish his allegation that preventable harm occurred and that the administration’s response lagged behind warnings he had delivered.

Trump retains the power—and the blame

The headline spectacle is a senior Republican “swinging” at Cabinet officials. The institutional reality is less convenient for Trump: Lutnick remains in office because Trump wants him there.

Trump has defended Lutnick’s handling of the Nvidia controversy and said he has no plans to replace him. Cotton’s formulation accommodates that hierarchy. He said that if Trump has lost confidence in Lutnick, the president should request his resignation. Cotton did not claim the authority to make that decision, because he does not have it.

This is the familiar structure of loyalty-centered government. Subordinates may absorb public criticism, but the president chooses them, protects them and decides whether failures have professional consequences. Blaming the Commerce Department without confronting Trump’s continued support for its leader would misdirect responsibility downward. Cotton stops short of doing that entirely, but his conditional language allows Trump to remain the final judge of an official whose performance Trump has already endorsed.

Cotton also argued that Trump should move quickly to nominate any successor while Republicans still control the Senate. According to the report, Democrats are set to take control of the chamber in January 2027. His urgency therefore reflects more than national-security policy: it reflects the partisan advantage Trump would retain in installing a replacement before control changes hands.

A dissent contained within Trump’s authority

Cotton says Trump has known his position on China since the transition before Trump’s first term in 2016. His criticism is therefore not the conversion of a loyalist after a controversy became public. He presents it as the culmination of a decade-long argument, including specific warnings delivered to the current administration.

But the senator’s challenge remains carefully bounded. He accuses officials of taking China too lightly, says the failure was preventable and calls for an assessment of the resulting damage. He does not call on Lutnick to leave. He does not demand that Trump reverse his defense of the commerce secretary. Instead, he offers Trump a timetable for replacing Lutnick if the president independently decides trust has been broken.

That is a sharp indictment of the administration’s conduct, but not a rebellion against its governing logic. Cotton has identified an alleged national-security failure, the official he believes mishandled it and the president empowered to impose accountability. Trump, for now, has chosen loyalty to Lutnick. Whatever damage the administration eventually catalogs will belong not only to the officials who allegedly ignored the warnings, but to the president who was warned and continues to stand behind them.

item.title: Melania tells Fox she’s 'not really' into Trump’s 'tacky' obsession
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Melania Trump did not call her husband’s gold-heavy White House makeover “tacky.” What she did, during a Friday appearance on Fox & Friends , was reject host Brian Kilmeade’s joking prediction that the Christmas decorations would feature “more gold.” Raising a hand, the first lady answered: “No. Not really.” It was a small exchange, but a revealing one: even Donald Trump’s wife would not endorse extending his gilded aesthetic into the holiday display. A joke built on presidential excess Melania
item.content:encoded:
Melania Trump did not call her husband’s gold-heavy White House makeover “tacky.” What she did, during a Friday appearance on Fox & Friends, was reject host Brian Kilmeade’s joking prediction that the Christmas decorations would feature “more gold.” Raising a hand, the first lady answered: “No. Not really.” It was a small exchange, but a revealing one: even Donald Trump’s wife would not endorse extending his gilded aesthetic into the holiday display.

A joke built on presidential excess

Melania Trump appeared on Fox to promote her new series about life in the White House. Near the end of the segment, host Ainsley Earhardt praised the Christmas decorations, and the first lady invited the panel to visit. Kilmeade then supplied the gold joke.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

It worked because Trump’s fixation is not subtle. According to AlterNet, he has added gold-painted molding and ceiling details, urns, coasters and a thick “Trump” paperweight to the White House during his second term. Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported in Regime Change that the president personally glued gold ornaments to the Oval Office fireplace.

AlterNet also reports that Trump proposed placing a golden winged figure atop a 250-foot triumphal arch and had a collection of Washington horse statues coated in gold. The recurring theme is less decoration than self-mythology: public space treated as a setting for the president’s preferred image of wealth and grandeur.

Melania’s “not really” should not be inflated into a political break or even a comprehensive verdict on the renovations. She was responding to a joke about this year’s Christmas decorations. But her dismissal punctured the premise that Trump’s taste automatically defines every part of the White House simply because he occupies it.

The People’s House as personal branding

Presidents inevitably alter the building where they live and work. The political question is what those alterations communicate. Trump’s additions turn the executive mansion toward the visual language of his private brand, complete with his own name rendered as décor.

That matters because the White House is not a personal resort or a monument awarded to its current tenant. Trump holds the institutional authority to reshape its presentation, and his aesthetic choices repeatedly collapse the distinction between the presidency and the president’s ego. The gold does not establish strength or prosperity. It advertises his preferred version of both.

The media framing around Melania risks misdirecting attention toward a familiar marital sideshow: Does she secretly dislike his taste? Is she rebelling? The reported exchange establishes only that she did not want “more gold” associated with the Christmas display. The consequential actor remains the president, who has used his control over the executive mansion to impose that aesthetic throughout it.

A carefully managed counter-image

Holiday decoration has traditionally fallen largely within the first lady’s domain, and AlterNet describes Melania Trump’s choices as mostly conventional. Some displays nevertheless became spectacles of their own. Her stark 2019 design was criticized as joyless; the 2018 scarlet trees prompted comparisons to The Handmaid’s Tale; and commenters likened the 2017 décor to the horror film The Babadook.

Her Fox appearance was itself part of another image-making project. The series she was promoting was produced and released by Jeff Bezos’ Amazon, which had already produced a documentary about her. AlterNet reports that the documentary held a 9 percent Rotten Tomatoes rating, while reviews of the newer series were harsh: The Guardian called it a “dead-eyed advert that barely manages to masquerade as entertainment,” and The Telegraph compared it to an “audition for a movie supervillain.”

That context makes the gold exchange more than idle banter, but less than dissent. Melania was selling a controlled account of White House life on a friendly network when an unscripted joke invoked the president’s conspicuous vanity. Her response briefly separated her presentation from his. It did not challenge the power that allowed him to turn the nation’s executive residence into another extension of the Trump name.

item.title: Trump teases a Stephen Miller 2028 presidential run
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: President Donald Trump floated White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller as a possible 2028 presidential candidate on Friday, publicly elevating the architect of his deportation agenda over Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The remark may have been improvised, but the power behind it was not: Trump had just called Miller “the most powerful man in the world,” an extraordinary description of an unelected aide whose promotion gives one of the administration’s most extreme
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump floated White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller as a possible 2028 presidential candidate on Friday, publicly elevating the architect of his deportation agenda over Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The remark may have been improvised, but the power behind it was not: Trump had just called Miller “the most powerful man in the world,” an extraordinary description of an unelected aide whose promotion gives one of the administration’s most extreme figures greater control inside the White House.

Trump stages a succession contest

The suggestion came during a White House press conference that wandered through potholes, former President Joe Biden, Republicans’ midterm losses and Trump’s relationships with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump dismissed critics of his friendliness toward the two authoritarian leaders as “stupid people” and insisted, amid the digressions, that he does not “ramble at all.”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

He then abruptly introduced Miller as “the most powerful man in the world” and invited him to speak. Miller responded with lavish praise, cataloguing what he called the administration’s victories and describing Trump as an “extraordinary” leader.

When Trump reclaimed the microphone, he gestured toward Vance and Rubio, who had been standing behind them, and announced: “Breaking news — he was better than these two guys!” He then asked Miller, “Do you want to run for president?”

The performance placed three potential successors into a loyalty contest controlled entirely by Trump. Vance and Rubio hold constitutional or Cabinet offices and have both been widely presumed to harbor 2028 ambitions. Miller’s authority comes from something more useful in this White House: proximity to the president and a demonstrated willingness to advance Trump’s harshest policies.

The joke rests on real power

Treating the exchange only as campaign gossip misses the consequential part. Trump did not merely tease a Miller candidacy. He advertised Miller’s institutional clout after installing him as chief of staff.

Miller has long been one of Trump’s most trusted advisers and, as AlterNet reports, a principal architect of the administration’s brutal deportation project. His elevation places a committed proponent of Trump’s most extreme impulses in a position to shape access, information and decision-making throughout the executive branch.

Whether Miller will actually seek the presidency is not established by the exchange. Trump asked the question; Miller did not announce a campaign. But presidential teasing functions as patronage in Trump’s political operation. He can raise a subordinate’s profile, humiliate presumed heirs and remind every faction that advancement depends less on formal rank than on his personal approval.

That is why Vance and Rubio’s awkward presence mattered. Trump turned senior officials into scenery while praising the aide whose power is least accountable to voters. The spectacle was unserious in form and revealing in substance.

Loyalty is the governing credential

A Republican succession struggle is already taking shape under the burden of the administration’s unpopularity. AlterNet reports that Vance’s political standing has fallen over the past year, while Rubio has received comparatively less damaging coverage. Polling released Thursday found Republican respondents preferred Rubio to Vance for the 2028 nomination.

One poll does not settle a nomination years in advance, and Trump’s question does not create a Miller campaign. It does, however, expose the governing hierarchy. Vance may be vice president and Rubio may lead the State Department, but Trump publicly presented Miller as the more impressive performer and the more powerful man.

Miller earned that praise immediately after delivering an effusive tribute to Trump. In this administration, policy radicalism and personal flattery are not competing qualifications. They reinforce each other.

The unresolved question is therefore not whether Trump’s latest provocation predicts the 2028 ballot. It is what Miller will do with the authority he already has. For people subject to the deportation machinery he helped design, that is the contest with immediate consequences.

item.title: Critics erupt with laughter over Melania Trump's claims about Donald's diet
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Melania Trump defended President Donald Trump’s fast-food habit during a Fox Business Network interview, insisting his diet is “good” and that he eats McDonald’s only “sometimes.” The response drew ridicule because it collided with years of accounts describing McDonald’s, KFC, pizza and Diet Coke as staples of Trump’s routine. But the exchange was more than a spouse minimizing an unhealthy menu: it showed a friendly television interview converting a legitimate question about an 80-year-old presi
item.content:encoded:
Melania Trump defended President Donald Trump’s fast-food habit during a Fox Business Network interview, insisting his diet is “good” and that he eats McDonald’s only “sometimes.” The response drew ridicule because it collided with years of accounts describing McDonald’s, KFC, pizza and Diet Coke as staples of Trump’s routine. But the exchange was more than a spouse minimizing an unhealthy menu: it showed a friendly television interview converting a legitimate question about an 80-year-old president’s fitness into lifestyle banter, then offering reassurance without meaningful scrutiny.

A denial tailored for friendly television

Fox Business host Stuart Varney asked Melania whether her husband’s diet was “really as bad as people say.” She blamed the perception on press speculation.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

“No, not it’s not,” she replied. “I think, the media makes those assumptions and those reports, but his diet — it’s good. He has sometimes McDonald’s, of course. When you’re traveling, it’s sometimes, it’s much easier.”

That answer did several jobs at once. It softened a reported pattern into an occasional convenience, cast contrary accounts as media invention and replaced a question about presidential health with a wife’s personal assurance. Melania said she also eats McDonald’s, though less often than her husband.

AlterNet reports that Trump’s customary order has widely been described as two Big Macs, two Filet-O-Fish sandwiches, a Quarter Pounder, fries and a chocolate malt or shake. The article does not establish how often he eats that meal. It does, however, cite a substantially older account from two former aides. In their 2017 book Let Trump Be Trump, David Bossie and Corey Lewandowski wrote that aboard Trump Force One, the “four major food groups” were McDonald’s, Kentucky Fried Chicken, pizza and Diet Coke.

Against that history, “sometimes” sounded less like clarification than image management.

Ridicule filled the vacuum left by the interview

Online critics responded with laughter rather than belief. One compared Melania’s claim that Trump only sometimes consumes McDonald’s and Diet Coke to saying he was “sometimes bald.” Another asked whether defending the diet was required by her prenuptial agreement. A third called the interview “a hostage video.”

Those comments establish mockery, not medical evidence. Their force came from the obvious mismatch between Melania’s casual description and the public mythology Trump and his own aides have helped build around his fast-food consumption.

Trump aide Natalie Harp reinforced that mythology while attempting to defend the first lady. She wrote that Melania was ensuring “a healthy balance,” then celebrated the way Trump’s preference for McDonald’s follows him abroad. Harp pointed to a recent Philippines visit during which the country’s president reportedly arranged a fried-chicken delivery for Trump’s team, exclaiming: “FAST FOOD AND WORLD DIPLOMACY!”

That is not a rebuttal to concerns about his diet. It is branding: the president’s habits become an endearing spectacle, and foreign accommodation becomes evidence of his cultural reach. The health question disappears beneath the merchandise-ready persona.

The unanswered question is presidential fitness

Trump says he is in “stellar health,” while critics contend that he is experiencing physical and mental decline. The supplied reporting offers no medical finding that resolves that dispute, and a fast-food preference alone cannot establish cognitive or physical incapacity.

That makes Varney’s framing especially weak. Asking Melania whether the diet is “as bad as people say” invites a personal defense, not an accountable answer. She is neither presented as Trump’s physician nor asked to supply medical information. Fox Business obtained precisely the reassurance its question was designed to produce, while Melania redirected skepticism toward “the media.”

The relevant power structure is straightforward. Trump holds the presidency. His family and aides help manage his public image. A sympathetic television platform gives them room to substitute familiarity for evidence. Critics on social media can laugh, but they do not control access to his health information or determine how candidly the White House addresses questions about his capacity to serve.

The result is a familiar form of political misdirection: scrutiny of an elderly president becomes a culture-war complaint about hostile coverage, and documented accounts from Trump’s own former aides are folded into a harmless fast-food joke. Melania’s “sometimes” claim became funny because it strained credibility. The institutional problem is that the interview never required it to withstand examination.
